description: Graduate Entrance Examination English study notes: Lecture 5: Negation and Emphasis. Original examples, diagrams, and exercises are retained.
searchText: lecture 5: negation and emphasis graduate entrance examination english study notes: lecture 5: negation and emphasis. original examples, diagrams, and exercises are retained. english graduate entrance examination english english grammar simple sentences 5.1 negation 5.1.1 negating lexical verbs what is a lexical verb? a lexical verb carries the main action or state meaning of the clause; lexical verb negative form structure: did/do/does + not + verb base form past events: did note: if the past tense action changes to negation, the verb should return to base form, then add did; present time: do present time with a third person singular subject: does give an example example 1: she likes music. she does not like music. example 2: american professors <u did not possess </u one. example 3: they do not fund peer reviewed research. 5.1.2 negating linking verbs, auxiliary verbs, and modal verbs method linking verbs, auxiliary verbs, and modal verbs become negative, directly followed by not be verb; modal verb; have/has/had, etc. in the perfect tense; examples with other audiences you <u mustn't</u attempt to cut in with humor…. directly add 'not' after modal verbs; ... average height…. <u hasn't</u really changed since 1960. in the perfect tense, 'has' is directly added to 'not'; when multiple words help form a verb, place 'not' after the first word such cooperation is likely to be stable only when each animal feels it <u is not being</u cheated. place it after is, not being; 5.2 emphasis 5.2.1 emphasis on finite verbs composition do/does/did+ verb base form; example: he does trust you he truly believes in you; although the figure may vary，analysts <u do agree</u on another matter… despite the differing figures, analysts do agree on this matter... the court <u did suggest</u that accepting favors in return for opening doors is “distasteful” and “nasty.” emphatic did stresses that the court really made this suggestion;

title: Lecture 6: Forms of Finite Verbs — Exam Strategies
description: Graduate Entrance Examination English study notes: Lecture 6: Forms of Finite Verbs — Exam Strategies. Original examples, diagrams, and exercises are retained.
searchText: lecture 6: forms of finite verbs — exam strategies graduate entrance examination english study notes: lecture 6: forms of finite verbs — exam strategies. original examples, diagrams, and exercises are retained. english graduate entrance examination english english grammar simple sentences 6.1 basic information core : 1. every finite verb phrase is marked for tense and may also express modality, voice, negation, or emphasis; 2. even when a finite verb phrase contains several words, the whole phrase is one predicate; 6.1.1 strategy 1: catch the finite verb core : grasping the finite verb means capturing the most essential expressive action or content of the sentence; examples …national spending on social sciences and the humanities as a percentage of all research and development funds….. <u varied</u from around 4% to 25%… core finite verb: varied , meaning “differed” or “ranged”; 6.1.2 strategy 2: locate the finite verb and find the complex subject core : by locating finite verbs, find complex and varied subjects; in an article, sometimes the subject can be very long. in this case, you just need to find the finite verb first to easily locate the subject; examples …<u national spending on social sciences and the humanities as a percentage of all research and development funds</u ….. varied from around 4% to 25%… subject: the underlined parts are all subjects; 6.1.3 strategy 3: judge the number of events by the number of finite verbs core : by the number of finite verbs, determine how many things are contained in a complex sentence; separate the events expressed in a complex sentence: identify each finite verb, then divide the sentence into the corresponding clauses or segments; finite verb: tense, modality, voice, and negation; examples the same dramatic technological changes that <u have provided</u marketers with more (and more diverse) communications choices <u have</u also increased the risk that <u passionate</u consumers <u will voice</u their opinions in quicker, more visible, and much more damaging ways. three finite verbs;

title: Lecture 7: Expanding Simple Sentences
description: Graduate Entrance Examination English study notes: Lecture 7: Expanding Simple Sentences. Original examples, diagrams, and exercises are retained.
searchText: lecture 7: expanding simple sentences graduate entrance examination english study notes: lecture 7: expanding simple sentences. original examples, diagrams, and exercises are retained. english graduate entrance examination english english grammar simple sentences 7.1 what is a determiner? 7.1.1 basic concepts what is a determiner determiners occur at the beginning of a noun phrase and help specify reference or quantity; common determiners and related noun modifiers: article: a、an 、the , etc.; numerals: one, two, percentage, fraction (e.g., two thirds), first, second, hundred, thousand; possessive/genitive forms: mary's , the company's ; note: nouns can also modify other nouns; examples <u the</u roughly <u 20 million</u inhabitants of these nations looked hopefully to the future. the marks definiteness; roughly 20 million specifies quantity; <u more than two dozen</u companies sell dna tests directly to the public, ranging in price from <u a few hundred</u dollars to more than \$2,500. determiner: more than two dozen : quantifies companies ; a few hundred : quantifies dollars ; merrill lynch got legal protection for <u an asset allocation</u strategy. the noun phrase asset allocation modifies strategy ; paraphrase: a strategy for asset allocation; 7.2 adjectives and adverbs 7.2.1 what are adjectives and adverbs? example introduction the <u angry</u boy shouted <u angrily</u . angry boys shout angrily; the first is an adjective; the second is the adverb; concept adjective adjectives modify nouns or function as subject/object complements; adverb adverbs modify verbs, clauses, adjectives, and other adverbs; both types add descriptive or limiting information; 7.2.2 how to use adjectives and adverbs method 1. their modifying functions; 2. positive, comparative, and superlative degrees; 7.2.2.1 adjective two ways adjectives modify nouns two common positions: method 1: attributive use directly before, and occasionally after, the noun; method 2: predicative use after a linking verb, describing the subject; the linking verb connects the subject and its complement; examples the idea seems <u promising</u , and rosenberg is a perceptive observer. these are two sentences promising is a subject complement describing the idea after the linking verb seems ; perceptive modifies observer, i.e., placed directly next to a noun; their thinking often had a <u traditional superstitious</u quality. their ideas often have <u traditional, superstitious </u characteristics; two adjectives to modify; 7.2.2.2 adverbs adverbs modify verbs, sentences, adjectives, or other adverbs (1) adverbs modifying verbs give an example most scientists and experts <u sharply</u dispute hardy's views. most experts and scientists strongly question hardy's views; and the right mental workouts can <u significantly</u improve our basic cognitive functions. in multiword verb phrases, an adverb may occur between an auxiliary or modal and the lexical verb; 7.3 past paper practice question : and where is the <u nearest</u water source? where is the nearest water source? question : they'll get <u less meaningful, less targeted</u ads less forms the comparative of both adjectives; the ads will be less meaningful and less precisely targeted; question : for the first time in history <u more</u people live in towns <u than</u in the country. +

title: Lecture 8: Prepositional phrases
description: Postgraduate English Study Notes: Lecture 8: Prepositional phrases. Original formulas, diagrams, and example questions are retained.
searchText: lecture 8: prepositional phrases postgraduate english study notes: lecture 8: prepositional phrases. original formulas, diagrams, and example questions are retained. english graduate entrance examination english english grammar simple sentences 8.1 what is a prepositional phrase? prepositional phrases are very important prepositional phrases are very important and appear frequently in graduate english exams ; 8.1.1 basic concepts of prepositions preposition : $prep.$ a preposition normally takes a complement; its complement is commonly a noun phrase, pronoun, or ing clause; followed by three types of words, forming prepositional phrases: 1. noun; 2. pronoun in object form; 3. gerund participial clause ( doing ); note: a preposition is not directly followed by a finite verb clause; a verb used as its complement normally takes an ing form; prepositional phrases commonly function as modifiers or complements; 8.1.2 key points 1. prepositional phrase = preposition + noun/pronoun/gerund (doing); 2. pay attention to the different meanings of each preposition; 3. prepositional phrases are an extension of the sentence; they are non core components but are very common content supplements; 8.2 how to use prepositional phrases 8.2.1 prepositions indicating time prepositions : at/on/in these differ by the type and scale of the time expression; at: time point (specific time); on: days and dates; in: within the time (year, month, season, morning, evening) preposition : before/after before/after... time preposition : from/since since... after time preposition : by/until deadline (until)... time preposition : for lasting... time preposition : during within a stated period or event examples <u on a cold winter's day</u , few culinary pleasures can match it. <u in march 1997</u , he lost \$72,186. in is used with a month and year; <u since the days</u of aristotle, a search for universal principles has characterized the scientific enterprise. since aristotle; 8.2.2 prepositions indicating place or range preposition : at/in/on at: a point or general location; in: inside an enclosed area or within a range; example: in the room ; on: in contact with a surface; example: on the table ; example: person lying on the bed on/in on: lying on a hard bed; in: very soft bed, sunken inside; the meaning of a preposition depends on the purpose of your use and can be used flexibly; preposition : on/above/over on... above on: indicates the surface of an object that is in contact; above: indicates various tops; over: indicates untouched above above the river surface; preposition : under/below/beneath in... below preposition : in front of/behind before... before after... afterwards preposition : near/by at... nearby preposition : beside/beside/next to at... beside it preposition : between/among between : usually for distinct, individually considered people or things, not necessarily only two; among : within a group or mass; preposition : around in... around preposition : into/out of/onto/off into： entering... inside: dynamic changes from outside to inside; in: to go, to be inside; into: the process of going inside; out of: movement from inside to outside; onto: movement to a position on a surface; off: movement away from a surface; preposition : across/through/past across : from one side to the other across a surface or area; through : from one side to the other within an enclosed space; past : beyond a person or place; preposition : along along with... preposition : from/to, towards from.../toward... going examples but many <u within the public sector</u suffer <u under the current system</u , too. many people in this public sector suffer under the current system; the link <u between</u dreams and emotions shows up <u among</u the patients <u in</u cartwright's clinic. information flows <u from</u the media to the influentials and <u from</u them to everyone else. information flows from the media to influential people, and from those influential people to everyone; 8.2.3 prepositions in other usages preposition : of ... of... (indicates attribute) a of b commonly expresses possession, composition, relation, or part–whole structure; two exceptions: a is a numeral or a measure word two of the students means two members of a particular group; the window in the classroom door describes a window located in the door; preposition : about about... preposition : with/without accompanied by with.../no... preposition : for purpose: for a specific purpose ; intended recipient/beneficiary: a gift for you ; reason: famous for its architecture ; preposition : by with... method, approach by bus: to get there by taking the bus; agent in a passive clause: passive voice + by identifies the agent; difference or amount of change: increase by 10 percent ; preposition : as role or function: work as an engineer ; comparison: as tall as ; in some fixed constructions, concession: as difficult as it is ; examples they perpetuate the myth <u of the lone genius</u . it also sent a clear message <u to</u the outside world <u about</u his aspirations. despite these factors, many social scientists seem reluctant to tackle such problems. despite these issues, many sociologists are still reluctant to address them; 8.3 past paper practice question : few <u of us</u just walk straight <u into the woods without a phone</u . of us: among us; into: to walk directly into the forest; question : <u for a time</u literature showed no interest <u in this public stage </u . for: can represent for..., can represent a period of time;

title: Lecture 9: Appositives and Parenthetical Expressions
description: Graduate Entrance Examination English study notes: Lecture 9: Appositives and Parenthetical Expressions. Original examples, diagrams, and exercises are retained.
searchText: lecture 9: appositives and parenthetical expressions graduate entrance examination english study notes: lecture 9: appositives and parenthetical expressions. original examples, diagrams, and exercises are retained. english graduate entrance examination english english grammar simple sentences 9.1 what is an appositive? concept an appositive is a noun phrase placed beside another noun phrase to identify, rename, or explain it; it adds supplementary information and may be restrictive or non restrictive; examples the number of papers including the keywords <u "environmental change”or “climate change”</u have increased rapidly since 2004. here, the quoted phrases identify the specific keywords ; 9.2 how to use appositives proper nouns vs. common nouns it said that internet explorer 10, the version due to appear with windows 8, would have dnt as a default. placement of appositives place the appositive next to the noun phrase it identifies or explains; 9.3 what is a parenthetical? parenthetical expression : a word, phrase, or clause inserted into a sentence and normally set off by commas, dashes, or parentheses; 9.3.1 subject–predicate structure as a parenthetical expression meaning : indicates "someone says, someone thinks..." no one, <u he submits,</u could have written it without possessing some power of reasoning. he submits: introduces the origin of the phrase; this speeding up of life, <u says the futurist</u , requires a new form of expression. accelerated life, futurists say, requires a new way of living; 9.3.2 adverbs as parenthetical expressions politics or, <u more broadly</u , the functioning of the state, is a major subject for journalists. 9.3.3 prepositional phrases as parentheticals justice antonin scalia, <u for example</u , appeared at political events. 9.4 differences between appositive and parenthetical expressions relationship : the two categories overlap, but they are defined differently; an appositive explains or identifies a preceding noun; a parenthetical expression is defined by its position: it is inserted into a sentence and set off by punctuation; example: tony, <u my teacher</u , is coming here. here, “my teacher” is both an appositive and a parenthetical element; example: tony, <u with his students </u , is coming here here, “with his students” is a parenthetical element, but it is not an appositive; reading strategy : non restrictive appositives and parenthetical expressions are supplementary, so you may temporarily set them aside while locating the core clause. paired commas or dashes often mark such material; return to the parenthetical information after understanding the main structure; 9.5 exam room guide strategy : how to use the core and extensions of simple sentences to improve your graduate english score? improve sentence reading and writing; write sentences: from short to long; girls playing games girls playing games lovely girls playing games thousands of cute girls playing games after class, thousands of cute girls are playing games on the playground; girls play games girls are playing games cute girls are playing games happily. thousands of cute girls are playing games very happily. after class thousands of cute girls are playing games very happily on the playground. grammar lets you expand a simple core systematically without losing control of sentence structure; reading: in a long sentence, temporarily set aside optional modifiers, identify the core clause, and then add the modifiers back; move from long to short to locate the core, then reconstruct the full meaning; sentence reading ability in response to these many unilateral measures, the organization for economic cooperation and development (oecd) is currently working with 131 countries to reach a consensus by the end of 2020 on an international solution. 1. find the finite verb to determine if it is a simple sentence (one thing): in response to these many unilateral measures, the organization for economic cooperation and development (oecd) is currently <u working</u with 131 countries to reach a consensus by the end of 2020 on an international solution. 2. simplify: remove the extended content: subject: the organization for economic cooperation and development (oecd) ; finite verb phrase: is currently working ; core: the oecd is working. 3. restore the modifiers and interpret the complete sentence;

title: Lecture 10: Non-finite verbs
description: Postgraduate English Study Notes: Lecture 10: Non-finite verbs. Original formulas, diagrams, and example questions are retained.
searchText: lecture 10: non-finite verbs postgraduate english study notes: lecture 10: non-finite verbs. original formulas, diagrams, and example questions are retained. english graduate entrance examination english english grammar simple sentences 10.1 non finite verb basic concepts the role of non finite verbs : a non finite verb can expand a sentence or serve as the core of a non finite construction; 10.1.1 what is non finite verb? basic concepts non finite verb： 1. still a verb; 2. but it does not exist as a predicate; why are non finite verbs needed? a clause is organized around a finite verb phrase. additional verb forms that are not coordinated finite verbs or heads of new finite clauses normally appear in non finite constructions; a non finite form does not show tense or agreement on its own; 10.1.2 when to use non finite verbs when to use non finite verb once a clause already has its finite verb phrase, an additional verb without its own finite clause structure normally takes a non finite form; three types of non finite verb in total doing when a verb appears as doing on its own, it is non finite; in a complete progressive verb phrase, however, it forms part of the finite predicate; 1. when used as a noun: gerund 2. when used as a verb: verb done when a verb appears as done on its own, it is non finite; in a complete perfect or passive verb phrase, however, it forms part of the finite predicate; to do in this use, it is non finite whether or not it appears by itself; two types of uses of non finite verb 1. core ingredients: equivalent to a noun , used as a subject, object, or subject complement (core component); doing/to do: these two can be used as nouns; 2. expanding ingredients: modifies nouns/sentences as attributives/adverbials (extended components); 10.2 used as a subject, object, or subject complement when a non finite construction functions as a subject, object, or subject complement, it is a core component of the sentence ; 10.2.1 distinguishing these functions method : a subject normally precedes the finite verb, an object follows a transitive verb or preposition, and a subject complement follows a linking verb; note : doing and to do constructions can function as subjects, objects, or subject complements; a bare past participle normally cannot function as a noun phrase in these positions; 10.2.2 doing and to do as subjects non finite verb doing/to do as subject change the verb 'do' to doing/to do, which can serve as the subject; example: <u laughing</u probably has little influence on physical fitness. non finite verb as subject expresses something, using singular in this case; if there are many things, you can use plural numbers; non finite verb can be combined with other components example: doing doing something： making friends is extremely important to teenagers. using 'doing' as the subject: on the other hand, <u putting your faith in the wrong place </u often carries a high price. the whole thing is done (putting) as the subject; use to do as the subject: <u to anticipate every imaginable driving situation</u is a difficult programming problem. the difference between doing and to do doing and to do as subjects, with little difference in meaning; main difference: different non finite verb position; non finite verb can be placed in front; a long infinitive subject can be extraposed to the end, with dummy subject it in initial position; example: put it in front: <u to anticipate every imaginable driving situation</u is a difficult programming problem. placed at the back: <u it</u is a difficult programming problem <u to anticipate every imaginable driving situation </u . place at the front: <u to do</u so is important. place at the back: <u it</u is important <u to do so</u . common forms: doing: in the graduate entrance exam, add more sentences; to do: in graduate exams, it is often placed at the end of sentences and referred to more often as 'it'; example sentence template: template: it takes sb. some time to do sth. demonstration: so <u it</u seems paradoxical <u to talk about habits in the same context as creativity and innovation</u . 10.2.3 doing and to do as objects position one: verb object : placed after transitive verbs; usage: both 'doing' and 'to do' can serve as verbal objects; context: after transitive verbs, non finite verb doing/to do serves as the object example: fortunately, the white house is starting <u to pay attention</u . fortunately, the white house is paying attention; the decisions made <u it</u more difficult for states <u to collect sales tax on certain online purchases</u . long objects can also be placed backward as formal objects; however, this can only be done when subject verb object complement is used, and 'it' is used in front to refer to the formal object; because if the structure is subject verb object, the object is already the last part, and there's no room for it to go further; position 2: preposition : placed after the preposition; usage: only doing can be used as intermediary ; example: the framers of the constitution envisioned law as <u having authority apart from politics</u . as: preposition, followed only by the object doing; <u thinking</u is essentially a process of <u making connections in the brain</u . of: preposition, followed by the phrase 'doing thing'; thinking: also a form of doing (doing form); 10.2.4 doing and to do as subject complements which forms function as subject complements: a form following a linking verb functions as the subject complement; both doing and to do constructions can function as subject complements; example: the trick is <u to direct these funds better</u . the infinitive phrase functions as the subject complement; supplement 1: a gerund participial construction can also function as a subject complement after a linking verb; supplement 2: 1. in a subject–linking verb–subject complement structure, both the subject and complement may be doing or to do constructions; 2. when both positions use non finite constructions, parallel form is usually clearest; example: yes seeing is believing. not allowed seeing is to believe. 10.3 used as attributives and adverbials when a non finite construction functions as a modifier or adverbial, it is an extended component of the sentence ; 10.3.1 basic concepts attributives and adverbials a non finite verb modifying a noun attributive; a non finite verb modifying a verb or clause adverbials; all are modifiers, depending on which one they relate to; non finite verb doing: indicates initiative; done: indicates passivity; to do: indicates purpose; 10.3.1 non finite verb as an attributive non finite verb modifying nouns, serving as attributives only by knowing the current modifier the noun being modified is the semantic subject can there be a reference know the active and passive parts; preposed attributives and postposed attributives 1. short ones are placed before the noun: preposed attributive; 2. place the long one after the noun: postposed attributive; 3. in chinese: any modifier noun is placed forward; example: the human nose is an (underrate) tool. 1. there is already the predicate is, all underscores are non finite verb; 2. the underlined part is between 'an' and 'tools', so it definitely modifies the noun of 'tool', preceding the attributive; 3. is the tool underestimated or underrated? the underrated underrated of the tool; full sentence: the human nose is an underrated tool. they include materials (sponsor) by energy industry associations. 1. should sponsor be non finite? the clause already has the finite predicate include , so sponsor must be non finite; 2. sponsor: who modifies? modifiers are materials (nearby modifiers); 3. is the material sponsored or sponsored by others? the back has by: so it is sponsored; be done and done: have the same meaning. if it is a finite verb, use be done here; if non finite verb, use done; 4. sponsored (done), indicates: materials sponsored by the energy industry ; it also raises questions <u concerning</u "values". concerning means that questions involve values, so questions are actively involved. so use doing; a team of researchers <u working</u together in the laboratory would submit the results of their research to a journal. a team of researchers actively working together, so it is working; permission <u to run</u a nuclear plant is a public trust. 10.3.2 non finite verb as an adverbial non finite verbs modifying clauses as adverbials example: in just one generation, millions of mothers have gone to work, (transform) basic family economics. 1. analyze the subject of the entire sentence: millions of mothers 2. did they change voluntarily, or were they being changed? it was they who changed the basic situation of the family; 3. transform transforming； supplement: if the purpose is to express an end, you can also use 'to transform': to change the basic household finances; （enrage）by entergy's behavior, the vermont senate voted 26 to 4 last year against allowing an extension. the senate was angered, so it was enraged; supplement: when done appears by itself, it is non finite; <u to test </u this idea, he turned to the university admissions process. people are…. poor at considering background information <u when making</u individual decisions. <u depending</u on the comments <u received</u , the editor would accept the paper for publication or decline it. 10.4 summary 10.4.1 method summary 1. a non finite form remains verbal but is not itself the finite verb of the clause. after identifying each clause's finite verb phrase, analyze other verb forms as coordinated verbs, heads of additional clauses, or non finite constructions. 2. there are three types of non finite verb: doing/done/to do, and 'to do' is always non finite verb; 3. usage of non finite verb: equivalent to a noun, used as a subject, object, or subject complement (core component) doing used as the subject used as an object following a transitive verb following the preposition used as a subject complement to do as subject: a long infinitive is often extraposed to the end, with dummy subject it in initial position; as an object: follows a transitive verb and cannot be used after a preposition; used as a subject complement after a linking verb; modifying a noun as an attributive modifier, or modifying a verb/clause as an adverbial (extended components) doing: indicates initiative; done: indicates passivity; to do: indicates purpose; 4. pay attention to the completeness of non finite verb phrases; 1. if it is a transitive verb, it should be followed by the object; 2. you can also add explanatory or modifying adjectives, adverbs, and prepositional phrases to form a longer non finite verb phrase. 5. conclusion: first, determine whether it is a non finite verb, then whether it is active or passive; an ed form may belong to a finite active verb phrase or function as a non finite passive participle; determine its role from the sentence structure; 10.4.2 exam room strategy tip 1: completeness of non finite verb phrases don't focus on just one word; find the entire non finite phrase; example: the <u networked</u computer offers the first chance in 50 years <u to reverse</u the flow, <u to encourage thoughtful downloading and... meaningful uploading</u . 1. in the networked computer offers the first chance , the finite predicate already exists, so any additional verb forms must be non finite; 2. a networked computer refers to a connected computer and is a passive non finite verb; 3. to reverse: the goal is to reverse this flow; 4. to encourage: the goal is to encourage meaningful downloads and uploads; tip 2: identify what the non finite verb modifies identify the noun or clause modified by the non finite verb; method: 1. directly modify nouns before and after by noun; 2. there are commas and periods to separate and modify sentences; example: passing the cafe, i saw a friend. passing by this café, i saw a friend; archaeologists commonly use computers <u to map</u sites and the landscapes around sites. to map: archaeologists use computers to create maps, so drawing embellishes the entire sentence; strategy 3: identify non finite constructions used as subjects, objects, or subject complements first identify the stable clause structure—subject, finite verb, object, and subject complement—then determine which role the non finite construction fills; method: 1. first, find the finite verb (tense, modality, voice, and negation); 2. use the finite verb as the dividing line: the subject normally precedes it, while an object or subject complement normally follows it; example: in adulthood, looking at someone else in a pleasant way can be a complimentary sign of paying attention. 1. find finite verbs, remember that a modal verb is followed by the base form, as in “can be”: in adulthood, looking at someone else in a pleasant way <u can be</u a complimentary sign of paying attention. 2. finite verbs are the boundary, and the preceding one is the subject: in adulthood, <u looking at someone else in a pleasant way </u can be a complimentary sign of paying attention. the doing construction functions as the subject; two prepositional phrases: at, in; 3. in paying attention, pay is after 'of' and uses non finite verb; the main purpose of this “clawback" rule <u is</u to hold bankers accountable for harmful risk taking and to restore public trust in financial institutions 1. is is the finite predicate; 2. the main purpose of this "clawback" rule; 3. subject–linking verb–subject complement structure, with the complement consisting of: <u to hold</u bankers accountable for harmful risk taking and <u to restore</u public trust in financial institutions; two parallel infinitive phrases: to hold and to restore ; strategy 4: retaining or omitting non finite constructions 1. if it serves as the subject, object, or subject complement, it is a core element and should be retained when simplifying the sentence; 2. used as an attributive or adverbial in a sentence, it is an extension component; when simplifying sentences, it is temporarily omitted.

title: Lecture 11: Compound Sentences
description: Graduate Entrance Examination English study notes: Lecture 11: Compound Sentences. Original examples, diagrams, and exercises are retained.
searchText: lecture 11: compound sentences graduate entrance examination english study notes: lecture 11: compound sentences. original examples, diagrams, and exercises are retained. english graduate entrance examination english english grammar complex sentences 11.1 how are complex sentences connected? simple sentences a simple sentence contains one independent clause; earlier lessons focused on structure within a single clause; long and difficult sentences learn how clauses are connected and how to choose the correct conjunction; what are long and complex sentences: multiple clauses and phrases connected in a single sentence; illustration simple sentences $n.+v.$ $n.+v.$ $n.+v.$ $n.+v.$ long and difficult sentences $n.+v.$ add conjunctions $conj.$ $n.+v.$ add conjunctions $conj.$ $n.+v.$ 11.2 basic concepts of compound sentences coordinate status coordinate clauses have equal syntactic status; compound sentences: 1. a compound sentence contains two or more independent clauses; 2. the clauses are joined by a coordinating conjunction, semicolon, or equivalent punctuation; list the basic concepts structure of compound sentences: multiple simple sentences + coordinating conjunctions; summary 1. structure of compound sentences: multiple simple sentences + coordinating conjunctions (the four types of coordinating conjunctions are the focus); 2. omission in compound sentences: identical elements can be omitted, while the remaining elements remain unchanged; 11.3 coordinating conjunctions 11.3.1 coordinating conjunctions expressing addition addition and sequence illustration pasted image 20240312122808 coordinates and ... and ... both ... and not only ... but also ... not only a but also b this pattern coordinates two parallel elements while adding emphasis; examples the renaissance was over <u and</u it was time for a new era—the age of reason. 11.3.2 coordinating conjunctions expressing contrast contrast basic concept: 1. the two things before and after are opposites; more goods are sold, but income decreases; 2. the second clause presents an unexpected qualification or result; note: in reading questions, important information often follows a contrast marker; common words however (a conjunctive adverb, normally separated by punctuation) ... but ... ... yet ... examples the environment is obviously important, <u but</u its role has remained obscure. we all understand that at some level, <u yet</u as medical consumers, we treat death as a problem to be solved. 11.3.3 coordinating conjunctions expressing alternatives alternatives choose between two or more possibilities; coordinates or (choose one) ... or ... either ... or ... neither ... nor ... (both alternatives are negated) neither ... nor ... examples <u either</u entergy never really intended to live by those commitments, <u or</u it simply didn't foresee what would happen next. 11.3.4 coordinating conjunctions indicating cause and effect coordinating conjunctions expressing cause and effect a reason may be introduced by for ; a result may be introduced by so ; coordinates reason ... for ... result ... so ... examples reporters tend to be part of a broadly defined social and cultural elite, <u so</u their work tends to reflect the conventional values of this elite. tend to be: often 11.4 omission in coordinated structures shared elements coordinate clauses or phrases may omit an element that is grammatically shared and recoverable from the first coordinate; retain every element needed for parallel structure and clear meaning; examples .... you don't“get”success but become it. note: if two coordinated clauses share a subject and the second subject is omitted, the second finite verb remains part of its clause; the program keeps track of your progress <u and</u provides detailed feedback on your performance and improvement. here, and coordinates two verb phrases; the later and in performance and improvement coordinates two nouns; omitted: the two coordinated verb phrases share the subject the program ; <u the program</u keeps track of your progress... <u the program</u provides detailed feedback on your performance and improvement. the peoples… ==died out== <u or</u ==became assimilated== <u and</u ==lost their native languages==. a coordinate structure may contain more than two coordinated verb phrases; the three verb phrases share the subject the peoples ; he must <u either</u sell some of his property <u or</u seek extra funds in the form of loans. the modal auxiliary must is shared by both coordinated verb phrases; expanded second coordinate: he must seek extra funds in the form of loans ; the federal government must <u support job training programs</u , <u raise the minimum wage</u , and <u fund more low cost housing</u . before omitting: the federal government must support job training programs； the federal government must raise the minimum wage； the federal government must fund more low cost housing；

title: Lecture 12: Noun clauses
description: Postgraduate English Study Notes: Lecture 12: Noun Clauses. Original formulas, diagrams, and example questions are retained.
searchText: lecture 12: noun clauses postgraduate english study notes: lecture 12: noun clauses. original formulas, diagrams, and example questions are retained. english graduate entrance examination english english grammar complex sentences 12.1 complex sentences introduction when two sentences are equally important, you can use a compound sentence; when one proposition is subordinate to another, use a complex sentence containing a main clause and one or more subordinate clauses; primary proposition: main clause subordinate proposition: subordinate clause the main focus is how subordinate clauses are formed and used. 12.1.1 composition of complex sentences composition analysis main clause: america's new plan to buy up toxic assets will not work. clause 1: <u unless</u banks mark assets to levels clause 2: <u which</u buyers find attractive. the main clause is a regular sentence, with a conjunction added before the clause; 12.1.2 classification of clauses section 1: noun clauses section 2: relative clauses section 3: adverbial clauses 12.2 what is a nominal clause? concept a clause used as a noun in a sentence is called a noun clause; four types of noun clauses 1. object clauses (most tested) 2. predicative clauses (slightly less tested) 3. subject clauses (also important) 4. appositive clauses (also important) similarities: the writing method is basically the same, just the position differs once you master one method, the other three methods are similar; 12.3 usage of object clauses 12.3.1 basics of object clauses what is an object clause core concept: a subordinate clause functions as the object of a verb, preposition, or adjective in the main clause; illustration: judge kennedy wrote that the previous resolution was flawed; pasted image 20240313195420 12.3.2 writing object clauses how to write object clauses core: 1. an embedded object clause normally uses declarative word order; 2. even when the main clause is a question, the embedded clause does not use question inversion; 3. in short: use declarative word order inside an object clause ; 1. turn a statement into a that clause add that before the statement and place the clause after the verb or expression that selects it; dr. worm acknowledges （that）<u these figures are conservative</u . that: although omitted, it is not recommended to omit it; we believe （that）<u consumers should have more control</u . 2. turn a wh question into an embedded clause keep the wh word, but restore declarative subject–finite verb order; we suddenly can't remember <u where we put the keys just a moment ago</u . 3. turn a yes–no question into an embedded clause add if or whether before the clause; whether is often preferable in formal writing; yes–no question: are other clients going to abandon me, too? answers generally only include yes or no; after revision: i don't know <u if other clients are going to abandon me, too</u .... 12.3.3 usage and position of object clauses summary: usage of object clauses common principles 1. embedded clauses normally use declarative word order; 2. a subordinator or interrogative word introduces the clause; method 1. put the embedded proposition in declarative word order; 2. choose an appropriate introductory word; 3. choose it according to the missing meaning or grammatical role: 1. time: when 2. place: where 3. person: who 4. complete statement with no missing element: that example: i know what you bought at the store yesterday; i know <u what</u you bought at the store yesterday. summary: position of object clauses core concept: object clauses occur in three common grammatical environments; 1. verb object: verb and simple object: transitive verb + clause; double object pattern: transitive verb + indirect object (person) + object clause; 2. object of a preposition; 3. adjective + object clause (just understand); verb + single object clause ... scientists believe <u that intelligence can expand and fluctuate according to mental effort</u . the that clause answers “believe what?” and functions as the direct object of believe ; ... users could tell advertisers that <u they did not want to be followed</u supplement: non finite verb + object .. she wanted to know <u if vaccines come from animal research</u . supplement: multiple object clauses to filter out <u what</u is unique from <u what</u is shared might enable us to understand <u how</u ==complex cultural behavior arose== and <u what</u ==guides it in evolutionary or cognitive terms==. what is unique : an object clause after filter out ; from what: preposition object clause; supplement: a long object clause may be extraposed, with dummy it in the usual object position; that kind of activity makes <u it</u less likely <u that the court's decisions will be accepted as impartial judgments</u it is the dummy object; the that clause is the extraposed semantic object; why is the object clause placed later: 1. in subject verb object object complement, the object is followed by an object complement, so keeping a long object clause in its usual position would make the sentence difficult to process; 2. the object is too long; 12.4 predicative clauses 12.4.1 what is a predicative clause? what is a predicative clause core concept: a subordinate clause functions as the subject complement after a linking verb; illustration: pasted image 20240314122836 12.4.2 writing predicative clauses how to write predicative clauses : the method is the same as for object clauses illustration: pasted image 20240314123004 note: 'that' in object clauses can be omitted, but 'that' in predicative clauses cannot be omitted; examples part of the issue is <u that</u airports have only so much room for screening lanes. part of the problem is that airports have limited space; this is <u where</u developing new habits comes in. this is <u why</u repeated attempts at reform legislation have failed in recent years. 12.4.3 position of predicative clauses composition subject + linking verb + subject complement common linking verbs: 1. forms of be 2. sensory linking verbs such as look , sound , and seem 3. verbs such as remain and appear a clause that follows a linking verb and functions as the subject complement is a predicative clause; the most common is following a form of “be” used as the main linking verb; examples yet the fact ==remains== <u that</u the merger movement must be watched remains : linking verb; human nature ==being== <u what it is</u , most people stick with default settings. the explanation for insensitivity to smell seems ==to be== <u that</u <span style="background: d3f8b6" the brain finds it inefficient to keep all smell receptors working all the time but can create new receptors if necessary</span . after the verb 'be', it is followed by a long predicative clause; 12.5 subject clauses this is an important exam point 12.5.1 what is a subject clause? what is a subject clause core concept: a subordinate clause functions as the subject of the main clause; illustration: pasted image 20240314123935 12.5.2 writing subject clauses how to write subject clauses : use the same internal word order as other noun clauses 1. in the subject clause, 'that' must be kept; 2. use whether , not if , for an initial subject clause; composition: pasted image 20240314124135 examples <u that</u <span style="background: d3f8b6" the seas are being overfished</span has been known for years. and <u whether</u the community's work contributes much to an overall accumulation of knowledge is doubtful. the opening and links this sentence to the previous one; it is not part of the subject clause; the entire whether clause is the subject of is doubtful ; 12.5.3 position of the subject clause composition core concept: the same subject clause can be placed at the beginning or end; their meanings are the same; first type: at the beginning of a sentence note: at the beginning of a sentence = placed before the finite verb, not necessarily at the very beginning (for example, the very front may be an and); second: place at the end of the sentence note: use dummy subject it , then place the extraposed subject clause later; supplement: initial and extraposed subject clauses can express the same proposition. extraposition is often more natural when the clause is long; it is not inherently “more advanced”; examples just <u how</u people think is still far too complex to be understood... the subject clause is at the beginning of the sentence; how: how people think about this is already far too complicated; natural reformulation: <font color=" 92d050" it</font is still far too complex to understand just <u how</u people think. <u what</u is needed is a technology of behavior... the subject clause is at the beginning of the sentence; this initial what clause is already natural; it is a technology of behavior what is needed is not a grammatical extraposition; it did not matter <u what</u was done in the experiment... the subject clause is at the end of the sentence (this is the most commonly used in graduate entrance exams); forward: what was done in the experiment did not matter... <u it</u is becoming less clear, however, <u that</u <span style="background: d3f8b6" such a theory would be a simplification...</span 12.6 appositive clauses 12.6.1 what is an appositive clause? what is an appositive clause core concepts: 1. an appositive/content clause follows a noun within the main clause; 2. it states the content of an abstract noun such as fact , idea , belief , or evidence ; note: not all nouns require explanation. nouns that require explanation: abstract nouns (facts, ideas) ; illustration: that introduces a clause giving the content of the preceding abstract noun; pasted image 20240314153819 12.6.2 writing appositive clauses how to write appositive clauses : use the same internal word order as other noun clauses place the clause after the abstract noun it explains; the most common pattern is abstract noun + that + declarative word order ; illustration: pasted image 20240314154104 examples evidence <u that</u <span style="background: d3f8b6" the lovelife program produces lasting changes</span is limited and mixed. evidence is limited and mixed. used to explain evidence: the lovelife program produces lasting changes. since plants don't have nerve systems, the chances <u that</u <span style="background: d3f8b6" they have consciousness are effectively zero</span . the that clause gives the content of the chances ; main structure: the chances ... are effectively zero ; for my part, i have no idea <u whether</u gilbert is a great conductor or even a good one. the whether clause gives the content of idea ; 12.6.3 position of appositive clauses position of appositive clauses core: placed after the abstract noun being explained; abstract nouns: idea, opinion, view, fact, evidence, question, doubt, reason, demand, theory, belief, possibility, chance, hope, contention, guarantee... examples in other words, they all share a view <u that</u <span style="background: d3f8b6" the international tax system has failed to keep up with the current economy</span . explain abstract nouns like view; but the idea <u that</u <span style="background: d3f8b6" the journalist must understand the law more profoundly than an ordinary citizen</span rests on an understanding of the established conventions and special responsibilities of the news media. 12.7 summary 12.7.1 key points 1. nominal clauses are divided into four categories: object clauses, predicative clauses, subject clauses, appositive clauses; 2. noun clauses generally use an introductory word plus declarative word order; 3. choose the introductory word according to meaning and grammatical role. use that for a complete statement; that may often be omitted in an object clause; 4. the four types are distinguished by their grammatical positions and functions; position of nominal clauses object clause verb object verb and simple object: transitive verb + clause double object pattern: transitive verb + indirect object (person) + object clause object of a preposition adjective + object clause predicative clause: after a linking verb (most commonly a form of “be”) subject clause sentence beginning extraposed after dummy subject it appositive clause after an abstract noun 12.7.2 why study nominal clauses when expressing a concept, it is often necessary to use nominal clauses when a sentence contains more information and a phrase cannot express meaning, clauses need to be used to convey information; many essay templates use noun clauses;

title: Lecture 13: Relative Clauses
description: Graduate Entrance Examination English study notes: Lecture 13: Relative Clauses. Original examples, diagrams, and exercises are retained.
searchText: lecture 13: relative clauses graduate entrance examination english study notes: lecture 13: relative clauses. original examples, diagrams, and exercises are retained. english graduate entrance examination english english grammar complex sentences 13.1 basic concepts of relative clauses 13.1.1 modifiers relative clauses and complex sentences a relative clause is a subordinate clause within a complex sentence; what is a modifier? a modifier adds information about a noun; 1. a word or phrase is often enough when little information is needed; 2. when more information is needed, a relative clause can be placed after the noun to identify or describe it; 13.1.1 relative clause basic concepts of relative clauses core: a relative clause follows and modifies an antecedent noun; structure: in english, which introduces a clause that modifies the preceding noun discipline ; example: law is a discipline that encourages responsible judgment. ; pasted image 20240316010531 antecedents and relative pronouns/adverbs give an example law is <u a discipline</u <u which</u encourages responsible judgment. before splitting: 1. law is a discipline. 2. a discipline encourages responsible judgment. a discipline : the antecedent being modified; which : a relative pronoun that refers to a discipline and functions as the subject of the relative clause; functions of relative words 1. introduce the relative clause; 2. perform a grammatical role in the relative clause while referring back to the antecedent; 13.2 use of relative clauses 13.2.1 writing relative clauses structure of relative clauses position: placed after the antecedent (n.). writing method: 1. start from two complete clauses that contain the same noun; 2. turn the repeated noun in the second clause into an appropriate relative pronoun or adverb, then place the relative clause after its antecedent; illustration: pasted image 20240316011330 13.2.2 antecedents and relative words choosing antecedents and relative words antecedent: a thing relative word: which/that antecedent: a person relative words: who/whom/that note: who may be a subject or object; formal english uses whom only as an object; antecedent: a person’s or thing’s (indicates all relationships between people or things, "someone's/something's") relative word: whose antecedent: time relative word: when antecedent: place relative word: where note: where can refer to a literal place or to an abstract situation, field, or context; examples 1. the antecedent is things or objects, and the relative word is which/that; teachers need to be aware of the emotional, intellectual, and physical changes young adults experience. use that or which : the clause modifies changes , which functions as the object of experience ; furthermore, the legal system and the events <u which</u occur within it are primary subjects for journalists. the antecedent events denotes things, so either which or that is possible in a restrictive clause; 2. the antecedent is 'person', and the relative word is chosen as who/whom/that; in france, shareholders <u who/that</u ==hold onto a company investment for at least two years== can sometimes earn more voting rights in a company. in france, shareholders must have held shares in the company for at least two years to be eligible for voting rights; shareholders refers to people and is the subject of hold , so use who or that ; 3. the antecedent is people or things, indicating all relationships between people or things; the relational word is 'whose'; it also pledged not to deploy ai <u whose</u use would violate international laws or human rights. whose use means “the use of that ai”; whose can express possession or association for both people and things; this, for those as yet unaware of such a disadvantage, refers to discrimination against those <u whose</u surnames begin with a letter in the lower half of the alphabet. 4. the antecedent is time, and the relative word is chosen when; it is difficult to the point of impossibility for the average reader under the age of forty to imagine a time high quality arts criticism could be found in most big city newspapers. fill in when; 5. the antecedent is 'location', and the relative word is 'where'; today, we live in a world <u where</u gps systems, digital maps, and other navigation apps are all available on our smartphones. 6. when the antecedent is reason , the relative adverb may be why ; the other reason <u why</u costs are so high is the restrictive guild like ownership structure of the business. 13.2.3 notes on relative words 1. every relative pronoun has a grammatical role in its clause; that may refer to either people or things; 2. with things, restrictive relative clauses may use which or that . a non restrictive clause after a comma uses which , not that ; 3. whom refers to a person and functions only as an object; who may function as a subject or object, while that may function as either in a restrictive clause; 4. when a relative word is used as an object in a relative clause (after a transitive verb or after a preposition), it can be omitted; 5. supplement: special relational word whereby = by which 13.3 restrictive and non restrictive relative clauses 13.3.1 basic concepts examples restrictive relative clause: he will call his friend who is working in london. non restrictive relative clause (absolutely explicit): he will call his mother, who is working in london. non restrictive relative clause (the antecedent is already identified): this trend, which we believe is still in its infancy, effectively began with retailers and travel providers such as airlines and hotels and will no doubt go further. category illustration: pasted image 20240318230310 13.3.2 supplement 1: restrictive relative clauses and appositive clauses differences between restrictive and appositive clauses appositive clause purpose: $\text{ explanation }:\,n.$ location: abstract n. role of that : in an appositive/content clause, that is only a subordinator and has no grammatical role inside the clause; a restrictive relative clause purpose: identify or describe a noun; position: after the antecedent noun, whether concrete or abstract; role of that : that refers to the antecedent and functions as the subject or object within the relative clause; examples one possible response is for classical performers to program attractive new ==music== <u that</u is not yet available on record. music: antecedent; that: relative word; 'music' is not an abstract noun, so it is followed by a relative clause rather than an appositive clause; and 'that' serves as the component, so it can also be shown that this is a relative clause; the ==idea== <u that</u some groups of people may be more intelligent than others is one of ==those hypotheses== <u that</u dare not speak its name. this sentence has two 'that' clauses, both followed by the noun and then the noun, so it is either an appositive clause or a relative clause; the first that clause explains the content of the idea , so it is an appositive/content clause; the second 'that' serves as a component, expressing... such an assumption, so it is a relative clause; ... we unconsciously imitate the behavior (<u that</u ) we see every day . the word 'that' here is omitted; conclusion: a noun + that clause sequence may be either a relative clause or an appositive/content clause; decide by checking whether that has a grammatical role inside the clause; 13.3.3 supplement 2: relative clauses referring to an entire clause special non restrictive relative clauses that comment on the whole preceding clause usage: 1. when adding to the whole sentence, only $\text{ comma }+which$ or $\text{ comma }+as$ can be used 2. which normally follows the clause it refers to; as may appear before or after the main clause in patterns such as as is known ; examples most fisheries are well below that, <u which</u is a bad way to do business. which modifies the entire previous matter, thus modifies the whole sentence; a few generative rules are then sufficient to unfold the entire fundamental structure of a language, <u which</u is why children can learn it so quickly. which modifies the entire previous matter; here, which is why is a fixed relationship and cannot simply be replaced with as ; nevertheless, <u as</u any biographer knows, a person's early life and its conditions are often the greatest gift to an individual. as indicates the whole thing; 13.3.4 supplement 3: preposition fronting in relative clauses formal pattern : $\text{preposition}+\text{whom/which}$ a preposition may be stranded at the end of the relative clause or fronted before the relative pronoun; after a fronted preposition, use which for things and whom for people—not that or who ; examples grade forgiveness allows students to retake a course <u which</u ==they received a low grade== <u in</u ... with preposition stranding, in remains at the end of the clause; with preposition fronting: grade forgiveness allows students to retake a course <u in which</u they received a low grade... ... commercial genetic testing is only as good as the reference collections <u which</u ==a sample is compared== <u to</u . as ... as expresses a comparison of equality; front to : commercial genetic testing is only as good as the reference collections <u to which</u a sample is compared. television is one of the means <u by which</u these feelings are created and conveyed... by which: through 13.3.5 key points 1. overview: a relative clause follows and modifies an antecedent noun; 2. structure: relative pronoun/adverb + clause; choose the relative word according to the antecedent and its role inside the clause; 3. classification of relative clauses: restrictive relative clauses and non restrictive relative clauses; 4. supplementation of relative clauses (1) the difference between restrictive relative clauses and appositive/content clauses (2) special non restrictive relative clauses (supplementary explanation of the entire sentence) (3) relative clauses with a fronted preposition

title: Lecture 14: Adverbial clauses
description: Postgraduate English Study Notes: Lecture 14: Adverbial Clauses. Original formulas, diagrams, and example questions are retained.
searchText: lecture 14: adverbial clauses postgraduate english study notes: lecture 14: adverbial clauses. original formulas, diagrams, and example questions are retained. english graduate entrance examination english english grammar complex sentences 14.1 basic concepts of adverbial clauses 14.1.1 what is an adverbial clause? overview of adverbial clauses overview: an adverbial clause functions as an adverbial within a larger sentence; adverbials: add information about time, place, reason, result, purpose, condition, concession, comparison, or manner; they describe the circumstances surrounding the main clause; adverbial clause: a subordinate clause functions as an adverbial and supplements the main clause; the added information may concern time, result, place, reason, and other circumstances; 14.1.2 writing adverbial clauses structure of adverbial clauses structure: pasted image 20240319120240 subordinating conjunction: 1. the clause after the conjunction normally has a complete subject–finite verb structure; 2. the subordinating conjunction indicates the logical relationship to the main clause; examples <u when</u ==the united states built its industrial infrastructure==, it didn't have the capital to do so. when the united states built its industrial infrastructure specifies the time for the main clause, it didn't have the capital to do so ; here, 'when' forms a time adverbial clause; we did not evolve, <u because</u ==machines and society did it for us==. because introduces an adverbial clause of reason; 14.1.3 position of adverbial clauses position of adverbial clauses : an adverbial clause may appear before or after the main clause, or parenthetically inside it. punctuation changes with position, but the basic logical relationship remains the same; three positions : before the main clause <u as</u ==the economy picks up==, opportunities will abound for aspiring leaders. as introduces a time adverbial clause; three positions : after the main clause opportunities will abound for aspiring leaders, <u as</u ==the economy picks up==. three positions : in the main clause opportunities, <u as</u ==the economy picks up==, will abound for aspiring leaders. 14.2 classification of adverbial clauses nine categories 1. adverbial clauses of time 2. adverbial clause of place 3. adverbial clauses of reason 4. adverbial clauses of result 5. adverbial clause of purpose 6. conditional adverbial clauses 7. adverbial clauses of concession 8. comparative adverbial clause 9. adverbial clause of manner concept : classify an adverbial clause by the logical relationship expressed by its subordinating conjunction and by the context; 14.2.1 adverbial clauses of time adverbial clauses of time : when / while /as before / after since / until as soon as by the time each time / every time the next time examples but in some cases, one marketer's owned media become another marketer's paid media for instance, <u when</u ==an e commerce retailer sells ad space on its web site==. but in some cases, one marketer's owned media becomes another marketer's paid media—for example, when an e commerce retailer sells advertising space on its website; here, 'when' introduces a time adverbial clause; in 1995 the united states can look back on five years of solid growth <u while</u ==japan has been struggling== communities throughout new england have been attempting to regulate short term rentals <u since</u ==sites like airbnb took off in the 2010 s==. since sites like airbnb took off; ...<u by the time</u 100 percent of the evidence is in, it may be too late. 14.2.2 adverbial clauses of place place adverbial clause : where examples now, rivals will be charging sales tax <u where</u ==they hadn't before==. 14.2.3 adverbial clauses of cause adverbial clauses of reason : because since as now that in that: because... examples however, <u because</u ==these connections are made through effort and practice==, scientists believe that intelligence can expand and fluctuate according to mental effort. because: an adverbial clause of cause <u now that</u ==you have developed a topic into a tentative thesis==, you can assemble your notes and begin to flesh out whatever outline you have made. 14.2.4 adverbial clauses of result common result patterns such… that…. such + (adjective +) noun phrase + that ; so… that… so + adjective/adverb + that ; so that…. can introduce either a result or, with a modal such as can/could/will/would , a purpose; examples we define such sold media as owned media whose traffic is <u so</u strong <u that</u other organizations place their content or e commerce engines within that environment. here, traffic means the volume of visitors or audience activity; so followed by an adjective: strong; transitions should connect one paragraph to the next <u so that</u there are no abrupt or confusing shifts. 14.2.5 adverbial clauses of purpose adverbial clause of purpose : with a modal verb such as can , could , will , or would , so that commonly expresses the intended purpose rather than the result; so that….. in order that….. examples in december 2010 america's federal trade commission (ftc) proposed adding a “do not track” (dnt) option to internet browsers, <u so that</u ==users could tell advertisers that they did not want to be followed==. so that + could introduces an adverbial clause of purpose; 14.2.6 conditional adverbial clauses conditional adverbial clauses : if unless: if not, unless once as long as / so long as examples <u if</u ==connections can be bought==, a basic premise of democratic society... is undermined the us supreme court frowns on sex based classifications <u unless</u ==they are designed to address an “important” policy interest==. if you see a conversation as a fight or competition, you can win by cheating <u as long as</u ==you don't get caught==. 14.2.7 concessive adverbial clauses concessive adverbial clause : concession acknowledges one fact while showing that it does not prevent the result in the main clause. in standard english, do not use but in the main clause after although ; although / though even if / even though while examples the defining term of intelligence in humans still seems to be the iq score, <u even though</u ==iq tests are not given as often as they used to be==. even though concedes that iq tests are administered less often than before; <u while</u ==the quality of legal journalism varies greatly==, there is an undue reliance amongst many journalists on interpretations supplied to them by lawyers. although the quality of legal journalism varies, many journalists rely too heavily on interpretations supplied by lawyers; 14.2.8 comparative adverbial clauses comparative adverbial clauses : than: used for the comparative form as ... as : used for comparisons of equality examples but phones run on batteries, and batteries can die faster <u than</u we realize. 'than' introduces a comparative adverbial clause; in the general population today, at this genetic, environmental level, we've pretty much gone as far <u as</u ==we can go==... 14.2.9 adverbial clauses of manner adverbial clauses of manner : as : in the way that; as if / as though : in a way that suggests a comparison or appearance; examples during most of his walking life he will take his code for granted. <u as</u the businessman takes his ethics. summary : the use of as core: as can introduce several kinds of adverbial clauses; category: time: while / when; reason: because / since; comparison: as ... as ; manner: in the way that; 14.3 summary 1. overview of adverbial clauses (1) meaning of adverbial clauses: a sentence used as an adverbial to express descriptive information. (2) how to write adverbial clauses: subordinating conjunction + a complete declarative sentence. (3) position of adverbial clauses: before the main clause, after the main clause, and in the middle of the main clause. 2. there are nine classifications of adverbial clauses. which type depends on the meaning of the subordinating conjunction;

searchText: lecture 15: the subjunctive mood graduate entrance examination english study notes: lecture 15: the subjunctive mood. original examples, diagrams, and exercises are retained. english graduate entrance examination english english grammar complex sentences 15.1 special sentence patterns basic concepts section 1: subjunctive mood; expressing hypothetical, unlikely, or counterfactual situations; section 2: inversion; connecting ideas while giving special emphasis to one element; section 3: emphasis; giving particular prominence to one part of a sentence; 15.2 the subjunctive mood four moods discussed in these notes the subjunctive is used for wishes, demands, hypotheticals, and situations contrary to fact; four useful categories: indicative : presents something as factual; conditional : presents a result that depends on a condition; subjunctive : presents a wish, demand, hypothetical situation, or counterfactual; imperative : expresses a command, request, or instruction; 15.2.1 what is the subjunctive mood? core idea the subjunctive expresses unreality or remoteness . past tense forms often mark distance from present reality rather than past time; a counterfactual describes a situation that is not true; test 1: compare the statement with the known facts and ask whether it is contrary to fact ; test 2: if it refers to a hypothetical situation, ask whether it is presented as unlikely to occur ; subjunctive verb forms the subjunctive is expressed through the finite verb phrase , whose form signals that the situation is hypothetical or counterfactual; 15.2.2 counterfactual if clauses how to recognize them note: not every sentence with if is counterfactual; many if clauses describe real possibilities; use ordinary indicative forms when the condition is genuinely possible; use counterfactual forms when the condition is unreal, contrary to fact, or presented as unlikely ; tips: the clause introduced by if is the conditional clause; the other clause is the main clause ; method: 1. backshift the verb in the if clause; present counterfactuals normally use a past tense form; past counterfactuals use the past perfect; for a counterfactual about the past, use had + past participle ; 2. use an appropriate modal in the main clause; main clause: would/could/should/might would : expected result; could : ability or possibility; should : expected or appropriate result; might : weaker possibility; choose the modal that matches the intended meaning; 3. unlikely future conditions often use the same main clause pattern as present counterfactuals; past counterfactual concept: use the past perfect in the if clause to describe a past condition that did not occur; clause pattern: if clause: had done main clause: would/could/should/might + have done example: if he <u had played</u last season, however, he <u would have been</u one of 42. if he had played last season implies that he did not play last season; the if clause uses had + past participle ; present counterfactual concept: use a past tense form in the if clause for a present situation contrary to fact; clause pattern: if clause: did/were main clause: would/could/should/might + do example: your prospects <u would be</u almost as dismal if arguments <u were</u even just competitions like, say, tennis games. if arguments were merely competitions, such as tennis matches, your prospects would be almost equally bleak. unlikely future condition concept: a future event has not happened yet, so it may still occur; these marked forms present it as especially unlikely; the if clause may use a past form, were to + verb , or should + verb ; clause pattern: if clause: 1. did/were 2. were to do 3. should do main clause: would/could/should/might + do example: if railroads <u charged</u all customers the same average rate…. shippers… <u would do</u so, leaving remaining customers to shoulder the cost of keeping up the line. if railroads charged every customer the same average rate, some shippers would choose another option, leaving the remaining customers to bear the cost of maintaining the line; the situation has not occurred; it is presented as a hypothetical future outcome; summary study goal: be able to recognize and interpret the pattern; direct questions on the subjunctive are relatively uncommon; conclusion: pasted image 20240320235945 15.2.3 subjunctive mood in nominal clauses basic concepts if the main clause contains suggestions, commands, or demands , the subordinate clause should use the subjunctive mood; whether it's a noun, verb, or adjective, if you want to express a suggestion, command, or request, you need to use the subjunctive mood; nominal clauses include four types: object clauses, predicative clauses, subject clauses, and appositive clauses; examples european ministers instantly <u demanded</u that the international accounting standards board (iasb) <u do</u likewise. this year, it <u was proposed</u that the system <u be</u changed: ... the main clause expresses a proposal; the subordinate clause therefore uses the mandative subjunctive ( be changed );

subject predicate inversion: in graduate english exams, you only need to master " subject verb inversion ," where the order of subject and predicate is reversed, meaning the finite verb is placed before the subject; two types of inversion: full inversion: the entire finite verb phrase appears before the subject; partial inversion: an auxiliary appears before the subject while the lexical verb remains after it; 16.1.2 full inversion examples among the 10 worst performers <u were</u ==some of the most populous states==, including texas, which was given the lowest grade (f) and has a disproportionate influence...... most populous states: the most populous states; were is the finite verb. the opening prepositional phrase is not the subject; the subject is some of the most populous states ; the full finite verb precedes the subject, creating full inversion. the structure: 1. connecting the previous and following lines, introducing the content of the subordinate clause; 2. gives prominence to the opening among ... phrase; implicit within tylor's definition <u is</u ==the concept==… implicit: included within...; is is the linking finite verb; here, the concept is the subject, and the finite verb is has been placed before it in an inverted structure; also unclear is <u why microsoft has gone it alone</u . emphasize unclear, so place 'also unclear' first: 'highlight unclear'; important sentence patterns : there be + noun meaning: existence the there be construction expresses that something exists; it does not express possession. concept: existential there is a dummy subject; the following noun phrase is the notional subject; there is a girl states existence, whereas a girl is there normally identifies location; there is a book on the table: objectively expressing an existence with a book on the table; extended sentence pattern : there be + noun + prepositional phrase meaning of expression: expresses location or scope example: <u there is</u a great deal <u of</u this kind <u of</u nonsense in the medical journals… prepositional phrase; in some instances, <u there is</u absolutely no relationship <u between</u the content of the article and the citations. use between to indicate the range; <u there will</u now <u be</u a seven day wait for the jobseeker's allowance. now: indicates the current stage; there has been a kind of inflationary process at work… …. but <u there have been</u controversial views about its economic. political, social and cultural implications. <u there may be</u more matches in the database.. combined modal: there may be supplement: be can combine tense and modal 16.1.3 partial inversion concept part before the subject, part at the back; how to select and perform partial inversion? the word order resembles that of a yes–no question; do you like it? you like it. do you like it? he likes eating. does he like eating? yes–no questions use subject–auxiliary inversion; method: front the auxiliary before the subject; if there is no auxiliary, add the appropriate form of do ; scenario 1 : the negative adverb or phrase is at the beginning of a sentence negative word: words that express a negative meaning;
