introduction emphasis in spoken language: expressing emphasis through tone and phonetic stress; in writing, english can use a cleft sentence to give one element special focus ; an it cleft contains a clause resembling a relative clause, but its function is different: it divides information into a focused element and a background clause; basic sentence patterns basic structure: it is… that… example: i love you. it is i who love you. emphasizes that the person who loves you is me ; i love you. it is you that i love. emphasize that you are the one i love; focus: the element between it is/was and that/who ; background: the clause introduced by that or who ; note : a cleft normally focuses a noun phrase or an adjunct phrase/clause. an adjective immediately after it is often signals an extraposed subject clause instead; examples we hear the more honest argument only in recent years <u it is</u only in recent years <u that</u we hear the more honest argument… 17.2 variations in emphatic sentences variations in emphatic sentences structure: it is/was… that/who… present time focus: it is... emphasize past events: it was... generally, don't emphasize future events; if you do, use it is... that is widely used; who is also possible when the focused element refers to a person; examples <u it is</u they, not america, <u who</u have become anti intellectual. <u it was</u not until the 19 th century <u that</u the newspaper became the dominant pre electronic medium... past matters, using it was ; emphasizing time: not until the 19th century <u it was</u only after i started to write a weekly column about the medical journals, and began to read scientific papers from beginning to end, <u that</u i realised just how bad much of the medical literature was. here, it was is used to indicate past events; highlights: the focused element is the long time adjunct beginning with only after ; 17.3 emphatic sentences and postposed subject clauses judgment : is it an emphatic sentence? method 1: reduction method remove the it is/was ... that/who ... frame and reconstruct the remaining words. if they form the corresponding complete proposition, the sentence is a cleft; example: <u it is</u this implicit or explicit reference to nature <u that</u fully justifies the use of the word garden... removing the cleft frame yields: this implicit or explicit reference to nature fully justifies the use of the word garden... ; method 2: elimination method if an adjective after it is evaluates the following that clause, the structure is usually extraposition rather than a cleft; example: <u it is</u worrisome <u that</u society is medicalizing more and more behavioral problems... worrisome is an adjective is postposed as a subject clause; 17.4 summary 17.4.1 knowledge summary subjunctive mood : expresses hypotheticals, counterfactuals, wishes, or demands 1. counterfactual if clauses 2. mandative subjunctive in noun clauses inversion 1. all inverted (focus on mastering the there be sentence pattern); 2. partial inversion (the negative word /only is at the beginning of the sentence; if is omitted in the conditional sentence); cleft emphasis structure and variation of emphatic sentences: it is/was... that/who... the difference between emphatic clauses and subject clauses; 17.4.2 requirements for three sentence patterns 1. able to understand; 2. able to write inverted sentences and emphasized sentences in writing;

a subordinator or relative word introduces a subordinate clause; 2. locate the boundary of each complete clause scope of clauses concept: use punctuation, connective words, finite verb phrases, and nesting to determine where a clause begins and ends; three useful boundary clues: 1. major punctuation may close a clause; 2. a new connective may introduce the next clause; 3. in a nested structure, return to the finite verb or complement that belongs to the containing clause; two common structures: type one: a chain of coordinate or sequential clauses boundaries are often signaled by punctuation and connectives; sentence 1 + conjunction/punctuation + sentence 2 + conjunction/punctuation + sentence 3 ... type two: a main clause containing an embedded clause sentence 1: (sentence 2&&&&&) end position: 3 separate the embedded clause while keeping the containing clause's core subject–finite verb structure intact; a proposed segment is normally a clause only if it contains, or is understood to share, an appropriate finite verb phrase; supplement 1: two cautions for coordinating conjunctions: 1. a coordinating conjunction at the beginning may link the sentence to the preceding discourse rather than mark an internal clause boundary; 2. if the material after a conjunction is not an independent clause, treat it as a coordinated phrase or as an elliptical clause sharing an element; supplement 2: if a connective joins words or phrases rather than clauses, do not create a clause boundary there; supplement : about verbs ending in $ ed$ past tense form may be a finite verb; past participle may be part of a perfect/passive finite phrase or a non finite modifier; method: check auxiliaries, subject agreement, and clause structure rather than relying only on active/passive meaning; sentence 1: some species of trees have been "read out of the party" by economics minded foresters because..., or... sentence 2: because they grow too slowly, or have too low a sale value to pay as timber crops. grow too slowly and have too low a sale value share the subject they ; today they argue that market prices overstate losses, because they largely reflect the temporary illiquidity of markets, not the likely extent of bad debts. finite verbs: argue, overstate, reflect punctuation: the first comma is useful, the second is not, because there is no finite verb at the end; that、and、if the principle of british welfare is no longer that.. if... that you can insure yourself against the risk of unemployment and receive unconditional payments if the disaster happens. in the idealized version of how science is done, facts about the world are waiting to be observed and collected by objective researchers who use the scientific method to carry out their work. main clause: facts about the world are waiting to be observed and collected by objective researchers. how science is done : embedded interrogative clause complementing version of ; return to non finite constructions after the clause skeleton is clear; focus on two aspects of finite verbs: 1. location; 2. quantity; example: …an inability to consider the big picture was leading decision makers to be biased by the daily samples of information they were working with. finite verbs: was leading, were working two things, separated into two parts; subject predicate structure, with the latter part being the relative clause: they were working with strategy 2 : when searching, look for clauses first; when reading, look at the main clause example: the dutch giant elsevier, which claims to publish 25% of the scientific papers produced in the world, made profits of more than £900 m last year, while uk universities alone spent more than ￡210 m in 2016 to enable researchers to access their own publicly funded research... finite verbs: claims, made, spent produced is a non finite past participle modifying papers ; title: Lecture 22: Split Structure
description: Graduate English Study Notes: Lecture 22: Split Structure. Retain original formulas, diagrams, and example questions.
searchText: lecture 22: split structure graduate english study notes: lecture 22: split structure. retain original formulas, diagrams, and example questions. english graduate entrance examination english english grammar complex-sentence analysis 22.0 introduction three types of special structures section 1: split structures section 2: nested structures section 3: parallel structures it is based on ordinary long and complex sentences with some variations; first restore the underlying structure, then apply the usual segment + simplify method; 22.1 what is a split structure? split structures overview: related parts of the core clause may be separated by inserted or postposed material; core: find division and restore coherence; method: identify the intervening material, reconnect the separated core elements, and then analyze the full sentence normally; 1. parenthetical split: temporarily set aside material marked by paired punctuation; 2. postposed clause split: move the delayed clause mentally back beside the element it completes or modifies; 22.2 parenthetical split structures 22.2.1 split structures caused by appositive and parenthetical expressions appositive and parenthetical appositive: identifies or explains the preceding noun phrase; parenthetical: structurally, inserted into a sentence for explanation; however: when analyzing complex sentences, there is no need to distinguish between the two. just recognize the inserted components; features: frequently paired punctuation ; examples bob liodice<u , the chief executive of the association of national advertisers, </u says consumers will be worse off if the industry cannot collect information about their preferences. the appositive between commas identifies bob liodice and supplies background information; after removing this part, the content is coherent: bob liodice … says consumers will be worse off if the industry cannot collect information about their preferences. count the finite verbs: says , will be , cannot collect ; connective: if clause analysis: bob liodice … says consumers will be worse off subject predicate structure; after segmentation: bob liodice … says consumers will be worse off after analyzing it, retrieve the appositive and parenthetical words and continue reading; these benefactors have succeeded in their chosen fields<u , they say, </u and they want to use their wealth to draw attention to those who have succeeded in science. remove the parenthetical phrase they say; these benefactors have succeeded in their chosen fields and they want to use their wealth to draw attention to those who have succeeded in science. analyzing finite verbs: have succeeded want have succeeded can be split into three sections: conjunctions: and, who these benefactors have succeeded in their chosen fields and they want to use their wealth to draw attention to those who have succeeded in science. yet it is precisely these non celebrity influentials who, according to the two step flow theory, are supposed to drive social epidemics by influencing their friends and colleagues directly. 22.2.2 split structures caused by postposed clauses concept three positions of adverbial clauses: front, back, middle; in translation, an adverbial clause may be rendered before or after the main clause according to the natural information flow; examples peter hardy, who sympathizes with the views of the energy sector, is resisting proposed changes to science standards for pre teen pupils. inserted part: who sympathizes with the views of the energy sector segmentation: peter hardy…is resisting proposed changes to science standards for pre teen pupils. who sympathizes with the views of the energy sector yet these creatures are members of the biotic community and<u , if its stability depends on its integrity, </u they are entitled to continuance. yet these creatures are members of the biotic community and… they are entitled to continuance. if its stability depends on its integrity branch points out that, even if a growing number of official guidelines and textbooks reflect scientific consensus on climate change, unofficial educational materials that convey more biased perspectives are being distributed to teachers. branch points out that … unofficial educational materials … are being distributed to teachers. that convey more biased perspectives even if a growing number of official guidelines and textbooks reflect scientific consensus on climate change. 22.3 postponed clause split structure examples contrary to the descriptions on record, no systematic evidence was found <u that</u levels of productivity were related to changes in lighting. clause: 'levels of productivity were related to changes in lighting ' explain the previous 'evidence' clause moved after 'was found'; after moving back: contrary to the descriptions on record, no systematic evidence that levels of productivity were related to changes in lighting was found. in 2005, ibm <u noted</u in a court filing <u that it had been issued more than 300 business method patents</u ... where there is a gap between noted and clause in a court filing; therefore, you can move forward: in 2005, ibm noted that it had been issued more than 300 business method patents in a court filing... 22.4 past paper practice examples what is being called artificial general intelligence<u , machines that would mimic the way humans think, </u continues to evade scientists split structures caused by parenthetical material; sentences are coherent: what is being called artificial general intelligence... continues to evade scientists. evade: to escape, to make... confused (this question uses this method) parenthetical element: machines that would mimic the way humans think explanation of the term artificial general intelligence; when one of these noneconomic categories is threatened and<u , if we happen to love it, </u we invent excuses to give it economic importance. noneconomic: having no economic value; inserted content: conditional adverbial clause when a species without economic value is threatened, we give it an excuse to make it economically valuable; though typically about two inches taller now than 140 years ago, today's people<u especially those born to families who have lived in the u.s.for many generations </u apparently reached their limit in the early 1960 s. especially those born to families who have lived in the u.s. for many generations explain the term 'today's people' in a limited meaning; concerns were raised that witnesses might be encouraged to exaggerate their stories in court to ensure guilty verdicts. clause: that witnesses might be encouraged to exaggerate their stories in court to ensure guilty verdicts originally used to explain concerns; but moved backward to the back of were raised; move forward: concerns that witnesses might be encouraged to exaggerate their stories in court to ensure guilty verdicts were raised this<u , though it fulfills the laws and requirements offuturist poetry, </u can hardly be classed as literature. this the content following the subject is inserted main clause: this can hardly be classed as literature clause: though it fulfills the laws and requirements of futurist poetry explain why it is difficult; if connections can be bought, a basic premise of democratic society that all are equal in treatment by is undermined government one more reason not to lose sleep over the rise in oil prices is that<u , unlike the rises in the 1970 s,</u it has not occurred against the background of general commodity price inflation and global excess demand.

title: Lecture 23: Nested structures
description: Graduate English Study Notes: Lecture 23: Nested Structure. Original formulas, diagrams, and example questions are retained.
searchText: lecture 23: nested structures graduate english study notes: lecture 23: nested structure. original formulas, diagrams, and example questions are retained. english graduate entrance examination english english grammar complex-sentence analysis 23.1 what is a nested structure? 23.1.1 basic concepts concept core: one subordinate clause is embedded inside another clause; a sentence may contain several levels of clause nesting; analysis: step 1: segment the sentence into finite clauses and identify the core of each; step 2: determine which clause is contained within which larger clause; an embedded clause fills a grammatical role inside its containing clause; step 3: interpret the outer clause and each inner clause layer by layer; 23.1.2 example analysis examples the great question is who should benefit from the analysis of all the data that our lives now generate. step one: count the finite verbs is、should benefit、generate step 2: punctuation and connectives who、that step 3: analyze from the outer clause inward first, identify the outer main clause: the great question is ... then identify its subject complement: who should benefit from the analysis of all the data ... : embedded interrogative clause functioning as a predicative complement; looking further inside: that our lives now generate : relative clause modifying data ; logical relationships: pasted image 20240414225207 it hoped they would learn how shop floor lighting affected workers' productivity. finite verb: hoped actively hoping finite verb; would learn finite verb; affected actively affecting finite verb; connectives: omitted that before they would learn , and how ; clause structure: it hoped [that ...] : the omitted that clause is the object of hoped ; they would learn [how ...] : the embedded how clause is the object of learn ; logical relationships: pasted image 20240414225818 if we are serious about ensuring that our science is both meaningful and reproducible, we must ensure that our institutions incentivise that kind of science. pasted image 20240414230326 23.2 past paper practice examples carnegie would be right if arguments were fights, which is how we often think of them. pasted image 20240415230458 a few generative rules are then sufficient to unfold the entire fundamental structure of a language, which is why children can learn it so quickly. pasted image 20240415230657 look from outside to inside, layer by layer first look at the main clause, then the clause; researchers admit that their study does not answer the question of how much businesses ought to spend on csr pasted image 20240415230926 the most famous of these efforts was initiated by noam chomsky, who suggested that humans are born with an innate language acquisition capacity that dictates a universal grammar. pasted image 20240415231111 for years executives and headhunters have adhered to the rule that the most attractive ceo candidates are the ones who must be poached. pasted image 20240415231411 here is a troubled business that keeps hiring employees whose attitudes vastly annoy the customers. pasted image 20240415231800

title: Lecture 24: Parallel structures
description: Postgraduate English Study Notes: Lecture 24: Parallel Structure. Original formulas, diagrams, and example questions are retained.
searchText: lecture 24: parallel structures postgraduate english study notes: lecture 24: parallel structure. original formulas, diagrams, and example questions are retained. english graduate entrance examination english english grammar complex-sentence analysis 24.1 what is a parallel structure? 24.1.1 basic concepts concept concept: parallel structure places coordinate elements in matching grammatical forms; features: 1. coordinate elements should have the same grammatical function and a consistent form ; for example, coordinate prepositional phrases with other prepositional phrases; exact wording may differ, but the structure should remain parallel; 2. use coordinating conjunctions or correlative conjunctions to connect them; a compound sentence is one kind of coordinate structure; common patterns: and , but , or , nor , not only ... but also ; punctuation: commas, semicolons in short: coordinate elements should be grammatically parallel; note: if multiple components are listed side by side and the middle conjunctions are equal, the preceding conjunction can be omitted and replaced with a comma; three step method: find parallel structures step 1: find the coordinating conjunction; step 2: look behind the coordinating conjunction to see what form the connecting content is; step 3: look forward for something in the same form as it about the number of parallel structures scenario one: if two components are listed side by side in a sentence in this case, you only need to use and to connect directly: 1 and 2 scenario two: if the sentence contains multiple components side by side, for example, 1, 2, or 3 components at this point, you only need to use the and component before the last sentence: 1 , 2 , and 3 or the five sentences are: 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 , and 5 24.1.2 classification of parallel structures four types of structures (1) parallel arrangement of nouns (phrases). (2) parallel arrangement of verbs (finite verbs, non finite verb). (3) parallel arrangement of prepositional phrases (4) parallel clauses and compound sentences 24.2 four types of parallel structures 24.2.1 parallel arrangement of nouns and phrases examples the english, the germans, the dutch and the french were investing in britain's former colony. find the subject find the finite verb were investing subject: the english, the germans, the dutch and the french < the four contents are listed side by side; illustration: pasted image 20240416212602 the networked computer is an amazing device, the first media machine that serves as the mode of production, means of distribution, site of reception, and place of praise and critique. image: pasted image 20240416212744 as: why do you serve? four types of services: 1 the mode of production 2 means of distribution 3 site of reception 4 and place of praise and critique. note: you can mark parallel content with numbers; 24.2.2 parallel arrangement of verbs concept note: finite predicates and non finite constructions can each form parallel structures, provided the coordinated elements have the same grammatical function; tips: to know where the juxtaposition in the current coordinating conjunction comes from, you can look at the first word after the coordinating conjunction (such as and) to assess its part of speech. the word in the first half of the sentence that belongs to this part of speech is the beginning of the sentence where the first half is being paralleled; examples the process sweeps from hyperactive america to europe and reaches the emerging countries with unsurpassed might. two finite verbs are placed side by side; illustration: pasted image 20240416213250 it allows us to have perspective on our lives the ability to not take ourselves too seriously, to laugh at ourselves, to see the bigger picture, and to see that things will work out. parallel structure; to do non finite verb parallel; pasted image 20240416213505 two and three dimensional maps are helpful tools in planning excavations, illustrating how sites look, and presenting the results of archaeological research all are placed side by side with the non finite verb (doing) that is followed by in; image: pasted image 20240416213723 the financial crisis has made it more acceptable to be between jobs or to leave a bad one. structure: subject verb and object complement subject: the financial crisis predicate: has made object: it (formal object) complement: more acceptable to be between jobs or to leave a bad one true object: to be between jobs or to leave a bad one parallel structure; image: pasted image 20240416214028 24.2.3 parallel juxtaposition of prepositional phrases examples ... he advocated freedom of thought and of personal expression. illustration: pasted image 20240416214159 two prepositions side by side, together modifying the preceding 'freedom'; mental health allows us to view others with sympathy if they are having troubles, with kindness if they are in pain, and with unconditional love no matter who they are. pasted image 20240416222043 so disciplines acquire a monopoly not just over the production of knowledge, but also over the production of the producers of knowledge. 24.2.4 parallel parallel arrangement of sentences examples the problem is not merely that people do bad science, but that our current system of career advancement positively encourages it. co conjunction: not merely... but... illustration: pasted image 20240416222413 the behavioral sciences have been slow to change partly because the explanatory items often seem to be directly observed and partly because other kinds of explanations have been hard to find. pasted image 20240416222621 however, <u whether such a sense of fairness evolved independently in capuchins and humans, or whether it stems from the common ancestor that the species had 35 million years ago</u , is, as yet, an unanswered question. two subject clauses; because the first subject clause is too long, a comma pause is used; 24.2.5 supplement: multiple parallel structures additional information concept: generally, when multiple parallels are listed side by side, only the last one uses and; examples the development of the elizabethan drama for the next twenty five years is of exceptional interest to students of literary history, for in this brief period we may trace the beginning, growth, blossoming, and decay of many kinds of plays, and of many great careers. for the time, attention, and money of the art loving public, classical instrumentalists must compete not only with opera houses, dance troupes, theater companies, and museums, but also with the recorded performances of the great classical musicians of the 20 th century 24.2.6 supplement: parallel structure without coordinating conjunctions examples “those first few days should be spent looking for work, not looking to sign on,” he claimed. 24.3 past paper practice examples in addition, new digital technologies have allowed more rapid trading of equities , quicker use of information at the speed of twitter ,<u and</u thus shorter attention spans in financial markets. step 1: coordinate the conjunction and find the parallel structure as and; step 2: find the parallel form; this sentence: thus shorter attention spans in financial markets consistent in form; step 3: find ingredients with consistent form three forks; 1. more rapid trading of equities； 2. quicker use of information at the speed of twitter； 3. thus shorter attention spans in financial markets； the court's ruling is a step forward in the struggle against both corruption and official favoritism. coordinating conjunction: both... and the court's ruling is a step forward in the struggle against both corruption and official favoritism. coordinating conjunction: either... or grammar , punctuation, and spelling can wait until you revise. coordinating conjunction: and connect the three components together, then use a comma to connect them; but we are now knowledgeable enough to reduce many of the risks that threatened the existence of earlier humans and to improve the lot of those to come. coordinating conjunction: and co component: two phrases for 'to do'; the point of a style upgrade isn't to become more vain or to spend more time fussing over what to wear. coordinating conjunction: or coordinated component: a phrase meaning 'to do' to become more vain to spend more time fussing teachers are responsible for teaching kids how to learn<u ；</u parents should be responsible for teaching them how to work. coordinating conjunctions: semicolon ";" in one case, many researchers working around the ancient maya city of copán, honduras, have located hundreds of small rural villages and individual dwellings by using aerial photographs and by making surveys on foot. first parallel structure: hundreds of small rural villages and individual dwellings second parallel structure: by using aerial photographs and by making surveys on foot 24.4 exam room guide strategy 1 : the key to resolving a split structure is to restore it into coherent sentences two types of splits: parenthetical split; shift the clause backward and split; concept: after finding the split, resolve the split sentence (remove or move) it to form a coherent sentence; example: bob liodice<u , the chief executive of the association of national advertisers, </u says consumers will be worse off if the industry cannot collect information about their preferences. temporarily set aside the appositive, identify the core clause, and then restore the background information; strategy 2 : the key to solving nested structures is to divide sentences into layers method: step 1: segment the sentence into finite clauses; step 2: analyze the outer main clause first, then each embedded clause; example: if we are serious about ensuring that our science is both meaningful and reproducible, we must ensure that our institutions incentivise that kind of science. pasted image 20240420223507 strategy 3 : the key to solving parallel structures is to clarify multiple parallel structures concept: 1. coordinate elements should have the same grammatical function and a consistent form ; 2. find the coordinating or correlative conjunction that links them; method: three step method step 1: find the coordinating conjunction; step 2: look behind the coordinating conjunctions to examine the sentence form and components; step 3: look before the coordinating conjunctions and find sentence forms and components that match them; tips: you can mark the number in the juxtaposition sentence to indicate which sentence it is; example: simply arranging a meeting, making a phone call, or hosting an event is not an “official act". parallel gerund participial phrases: arranging a meeting making a phone call hosting an event why is the finite verb singular is ? the alternatives joined by or are treated here as individual possible activities, and the final alternative nearest the verb is singular; strategy 4 : graduate exam past paper question, always ask questions in difficult sentences example: as a linguist, he acknowledges that all varieties of human language, including non standard ones like black english, can be powerfully expressive there exists no language or dialect in the world that cannot convey complex ideas. step 1: find the finite verb acknowledges: acknowledges can be: modal verb, following the base form of the verb exists cannot convey: to negate step 2: find punctuation and conjunctions dash: one dash is for explanation; two commas: parenthetical words, can be removed; that: connector after segmentation: 1. as a linguist, he acknowledges 2. that all varieties of human language, ......, can be powerfully expressive inserted sections: including non standard ones like black english 3. there exists no language or dialect in the world 4. that cannot convey complex ideas modifies no language or dialect ; this restrictive relative clause completes the meaning of the antecedent; it is not a movable parenthetical; young people who are still getting started in life were more likely than older adults to prioritize personal fulfillment in their work, to believe they will advance their careers most by regularly changing jobs, to favor communities with more public services and a faster pace of life, to agree that couples should be financially secure before getting married or having children, and to maintain that children are best served by two parents working outside the home... typical parallel structures; title: Lecture 1: Reading Methodology

searchText: lecture 1: reading methodology graduate entrance examination english study notes: lecture 1: reading methodology. original examples, diagrams, and exercises are retained. english graduate entrance examination english english reading past papers, 1996–2003 introduced in 1.0 main components of reading methods (1) analysis of the question stem; (2) logical analysis of the article; (3) analysis of option issues; 1.1 method one: analyze the content of the question stem main direction : topic first, text later benefits anticipating the central idea of the article; method only look at the question stem, not the options; because there are five questions, one question has four options, totaling 20 pieces of information; so you can be misled by information, so just look at the question stem, which is less information and more accurate; 1.1.1 positional keywords concept : designated terminology concept: the order of the article's content roughly matches the order of the locator words in the question stem; use locator words to find the content corresponding to the question; category: 1. uppercase, personal name, place name, time, year, number 2. nouns, adjectives; 1.1.2 analyze logic core purpose : understand the general logic of the article and simplify the text; method : connect the logic between the questions and infer the article's theme cause: in the eyes of the question setter, it is definitely placed in important information; so with five question stems, it's most likely important information; the content that still appears repeatedly is most likely the central message; conclusion: (1) the information in the question stem is the most important information in the article; (2) the repeatedly appearing information in the question stem is the central message of the article; (3) if there is no repeated information in the text, at least you can read the article with questions in mind; example: question: 41. how did redmon find his job ? 42. which of the following can be a disadvantage of search agents ？ 43. the expression "tip service" (line 3, paragraph 3) most probably means 44. why does careersite's agent offer each job hunter only three job options? 45. which of the following is true according to the text? analysis: recurring keywords: agents, job information provided in question four: agents are used to help people find jobs; example: question: 21. which of the following is true according to the first two paragraphs? [a] women are biologically more vulnerable to stress . [b] women are still suffering much stress caused by men. [c] women are more experienced than men in coping with stress . [d] men and women show different inclinations when faced with stress . 22. dr. yehuda's research suggests that women [a] need extra doses of chemicals to handle stress . [b] have limited capacity for tolerating stress . [c] are more capable of avoiding stress . [d] are exposed to more stress . 23. according to paragraph 4, the stress women confront tends to be 24. the sentence "| lived from paycheck to paycheck." (line 6, para. 5) show that 25. which of the following would be the best title for the text? [a] strain of stress: noway out? [b] responses to stress: gender difference [c] stress analysis: whatchemicals say [d] gender inequality: womenunder stress analysis: why do 21. questions require reading options? conclusion: if the question asks which of the following information is correct, then the content that appears repeatedly (or even all) in the options is correct and important; core keywords: stress , women 23. appears: stress , women repeated information: women's stress 1.2 method two: analyze the article's logic reading logic : analyze important and secondary information important information recurring key content, focusing on key exam points; secondary information 1.2.1 focus on attitude method : you need to grasp the author's attitude method: two types of words in the article are key: 1. adjective; 2. adverb; by looking for the above two types of words, analyze the author's attitude; cause: reading comprehension refers to the author's attitude toward an event. these things are reflected in the adjectives and adverbs of the article, so when reading and understanding the article's logic, the most important thing is the adjectives in the article; genre: 1. is the relationship positive or negative ; 2. is the matter up or down ; 3. is logic denial or affirmation ; by judging the author's attitude, simplify the content of the article; method : look at modal verbs concept: modal verbs express the author's viewpoint and are also very meaningful; modal verbs can express strong emotions and thus emphasize key points; 1.2.2 logical analysis concept : analyze logic concept: when reading articles, you should analyze the translation based on logic; three types of logic to analyze: 1. sentence logic; 2. intersentence logic; 3. intersection logic; 1. intersentence logic; there are only two types of relationships between sentences; 1. same; multiple sentences repeating the same content is the central idea of the article; 2. on the contrary; but、yet、however ； 2. intersection logic; interparagraph prompt: the correct answers to different options are connected; logical analysis: analyze the logic of the content within the paragraph total score, sub total, all examples, arguments, supplementary information; 1.2.3 analyzing cause and effect relationship one : causality because of causal word: because because answers whatever is asked, looking for content in the original text; since as a preposition: since then as a conjunction: because as as a preposition: as as a conjunction: because for as a preposition: for as a conjunction: because method: the above causal words, when used as conjunctions in a sentence, should all be translated as because ; when these words are followed by sentences or finite verbs, this causality serves as a conjunction; relationship two : causality causes causal word: derive from originate from stem from result from method: these words are all followed by 'from', so the 'cause' is followed by 'reason'; relationship three : causality attribution + cause causal word: owing to due to attribute to contribute to core four : attributive clauses can express causality (explanation) 1.2.4 punctuation punctuation : comma concept: between two commas, or after a comma, a supplementary explanatory component non main content punctuation : colon concept: before and after the colon, generally moving from abstract to concrete, the content after the colon explains the previous content; tips: in sentences, its meaning is equivalent to an equal sign, equal in meaning to the previous sentence; punctuation : semicolon concept: the semicolon is arranged in a parallel relationship; punctuation : quotation marks concept: 1. quote; 2. irony or semantic transfer; 1.3 method 3: option analysis summary : about english questions question type: there are six main question types in the graduate entrance exam: (1) inference questions; (2) detail questions; (3) example questions; (4) core idea questions except for detailed questions, other types of questions have some typical markings in the question stem, which can be used to identify question types; difficulty: simple questions can be easily found in the original text; difficult questions content that is difficult to find in the article; core: all can be found in articles; option one word by word in the original text; question approach correct answer: the correct option for the question is easy to design, since you can just look it up in the original text; incorrect answer: wrong answers are difficult to design because they must be misleading and strongly linked to the correct answer; question approach: question approach for wrong answers: the opposite meaning of the correct option, partial incorrect error of the correct option problem solving principles: details follow the main idea ; tips 1. among options, if the two options have opposite meanings, the correct answer is usually the answer; the underlying logic of the proposition: attitude toward the proposition: the correct option is usually the one you don't want you to choose. the distracting option is usually what you want you to choose, which is something you can judge with common sense; 2. principles for the correct answer: (1) the answer that fits the central point is correct; (2) the most comprehensive answer is the correct answer; 3. should represents the opposite logic; practice methods write the questions twice; first round: do it directly; second round: follow the notes and redo the process; 1.3.1 reasoning problems features vocabulary: imply/implied/infer from.../because... method: since the chosen content is an inferential conclusion, to find a suitable option that can serve as an inference, you can analyze the positioning point described in the current problem and what the supporting viewpoint is. among the options, the one that matches this viewpoint is the correct one; core : when you need to choose an answer in abcd, it does not require selecting the "correct answer," but rather the " most appropriate answer " that is: find recurring and emphasized content mnemonic: the key points that appear repeatedly are the key points; the key points are the exam points; method (1) step 1: find the locator term for the current problem and locate the original text; (2) step 2: eliminate obviously impossible wrong options; (3) step 3: from the remaining options, select the best option objective principle; summary : characteristics of correct answers core: details obey the main idea; tips: 1. synonym paraphrasing tests vocabulary size; 2. closely related to the central idea abcd choose whichever of the four options is closest to the central idea recurring information is emphasized; 3. gentle tone: some, may, partly most likely correct; summary : characteristics of the interference options 1. confusing the positives and inversions; 2. concept substitution half right, half wrong; 3. answer irrelevant questions the content of the answers is correct, but not the question itself therefore, the focus of attention should not be on "comparing each option with the article" one by one; the core should be to pay attention to the question read the question first; 4. different content is grafted although the information is found, the answer is indeed incorrect for example, an option in the article has a but relationship but becomes or in the option; 5. not the best answer; 6. absolutized terms: only、must、exclusively、never、all usually not selected unless similar absolutized terms appear in the article; 1.3.3 example problems concept logo: example、case、illustrate、demonstrate、to show、to method: concept: the example itself is not important; what matters is the viewpoint it supports ; example questions are not detail questions, so the answer is not in the details ; even if you locate an example, it is not the answer; the key to answering is to find the viewpoints supported by these examples, and then solve the problem based on those viewpoints ; location: viewpoints are generally placed before and sometimes after examples; in the options, find synonymous substitutions for the content of the viewpoint; steps: (1) determine whether the current problem is an example question; (2) determine the starting and ending positions of the example; (3) determine the position of the viewpoint, whether it comes first or later; supplement: how to design distraction options focus on the issue, and within the options, discuss the example itself; some examples also need to be read to help us exclude them; give an example the author wants to prove with the example of isaac newton that judgment of opinions non viewpoint judgment: judgment: in the original text, it appears: such、this、that、those、these a class of words. when followed by a noun, it indicates that the concept of the noun has already appeared earlier; example: if introducing new content, the word this is not used right away; only when it is mentioned the second time can this be used; judgment of opinion: judgment: 1. modal verb after the content: should、could、would、may、might、must、need to、ought to ; 2. emotional color especially strong adjectives and adverbs ; summary interference options: switching between active and passive roles; vocabulary: lest indicates causality; 1.3.4 central idea questions concept logo: mainly about/discuss/the best title/purpose/appropriate title method: 1. wiring method: scope of application: universal applicability; method: connect the opening and closing lines of each paragraph into a whole, paying attention to the transitions; a paragraph also has a central paragraph, usually at the beginning of the paragraph so if you link the beginning together, you can capture important information; therefore, by linking the first sentence, a lot of secondary information can be filtered out; 2. central sentence: scope of application: look at the form; method: (1) center questions: the question at the beginning and the answer to the question are the central part of the article; (2) single sentence paragraph: a paragraph consists of only one sentence; 3. keywords: scope of application: most intuitive; method: words that appear frequently in the text; note: 1. often, it is a synonymous rewriting; 2. recent trends in graduate entrance exams: several high frequency words appear simultaneously in an article; supplement: when a viewpoint has two sides, graduate exams usually emphasize only one side; technique : central idea questions interfere with the characteristics of the options 1. the scope is too small one sided there are 1, 2, 3, and 4 points, but only 1 point is mentioned; 2. the scope is too broad looking back essay features: this is more disruptive method: use the four headings a, b, c, and d respectively, and use them to brainstorm a practical writing task; 1.3.5 author attitude question example : the author's attitude toward the issue of "science vs. anti science" is ? example : how do the public feel about the current economic situation? concept logo: attitude/deem/consider/tone method 1: summarize option vocabulary (1) positive vocabulary: positive/optimistic/approval/supportive (2) negative vocabulary: negative/pessimistic/disapproval/critical/doubtful/suspicious/skeptical/questionable (3) neutral vocabulary: neutral/objective/impartial/disinterested (4) incorrect option vocabulary: uninterested/unconcerned/indifferent/puzzled/subjective/confused/biased/prejudice/contemptuous method 2: when the author's stance is not clearly stated (1) the framework of the article; the article mainly contains positive/negative words positive/negative expressions; (2) adjective, adverb: adj/adv (3) turning points (4) after modal verbs: should/must/could... 1.3.6 vocabulary questions example : the word "schism" (line 3, paragraph 1) in the context probably means ? example : by"ellen spero isn't biting her nails just yet" (line 1 paragraph 1), the author means concept logo: "???" + (line .paragraph) + most probably means note: the object of word guessing in vocabulary questions does not have to be a single word, but it can also be a sentence. but their logic is the same, understanding their meaning within contextual logic; method: use well positioned sentences to match synonyms or antonyms based on logical relationships; features of interference options: literal understanding eliminate the most common meanings; tips: when the noun is unfamiliar: sb/sth when the verb is unrecognizable: do examples title: by"ellen spero isn't biting her nails just yet" (line 1 paragraph 1), the author means original text: when it comes to the slowing economy, ellen spero isn't biting her nails just yet but the 47 year old manicurist isn't cutting, filling or polishing as many nail as she'd like to, either. analysis: the 47 year old manicurist isn't cutting, filling or polishing as many nail as she'd like to, either. negative attitude; deduced when it comes to the slowing economy, ellen spero isn't biting her nails just yet : a positive attitude; 1.3.7 true/false concept logo: infer/learn from/imply/suggest/conclude method: 1. tautology: detail/main idea/logic; details: if the question is in the original text, then directly select the one mentioned in the original text this becomes a detail question; subject: if the original text does not include it, then choose the most appropriate option based on the main point; 2. logic is the opposite reasoning often occurs at turning points; tips: excluding absolutism and opting for a softer tone option but now it doesn't quite hold up; 1.4 article explanation: 2000 text 1 step one : connect the information in the question stem and analyze the key points of the article 51. the u.s.achieved its predominance after world war because. 52. the loss of u.s. predominance in the world economy in the 1980 s is manifested in the fact that theamerican 53. what can be inferred from the passage? 54. the author seems to believe the revival of the useconomy in the 1990 s can be attributed to the. from points 51 and 52, it is clear that "us economic predominance" is the core of the article discussing economic changes in the article; at first, it was fine, then it didn't work, and then it revived; provides a sense of direction; step 2 : read the article with questions in mind question: 51. the u.s.achieved its predominance after world war because. content: a history of long and effortless success can be a dreadful handicap, but, if properly handled, it may become a driving force. when the united states entered just such a glowing period after the end of the second world war, it had a market eight times larger than any competitor, giving its industries unparalleled economies of scale. its scientists were the world's best; its workers the most skilled. america and americans were prosperous beyond the dreams of the europeans and asians whose economies the war had destroyed. analysis: logic within sentences a history of long and effortless success can be a dreadful handicap, but, if properly handled, it may become a driving force. translate first analyze logic; vocabulary in it: dreadful and the author's attitude toward it: although not good, it can be good; besides translation, you also need to analyze logic; summary: conducting logical analysis based on the basics of translation; three types of logic to analyze: 1. sentence logic; 2. intersentence logic; 3. intersection logic; reading the author's attitude: reading comprehension refers to the author's attitude toward an event. these things are reflected in the adjectives and adverbs of the article, so when reading and understanding the article's logic, the most important thing is the adjectives in the article; analysis: logic within sentences when the united states entered just such a glowing period after the end of the second world war, it had a market eight times larger than any competitor, giving its industries unparalleled economies of scale. its scientists were the world's best; its workers the most skilled. america and americans were prosperous beyond the dreams of the europeans and asians whose economies the war had destroyed. analysis: when the united states entered just such a glowing period after the end of the second world war, it had a market eight times larger than any competitor, giving its industries unparalleled economies of scale. its scientists were the world's best; its workers the most skilled. the united states is developing exceptionally well; america and americans were prosperous beyond the dreams of the europeans and asians whose economies the war had destroyed. the united states is developing very well and is the dream of people in asia and europe; intersentence logic analysis: all four sentences above express the same thing, so they can be considered equal; why repeat the same thing four times because important things are repeated so that's the central idea of the article; summary: intersentence logic there are only two types of relationships between sentences; 1. same; multiple sentences repeating the same content is the central idea of the article; 2. on the contrary; but、yet、however； step 3 : solving the problem question 1 question: 51. the u.s.achieved its predominance after world war because. [a] it had made painstaking efforts towards this goal [b] its domestic market was eight times larger than before [c] the war had destroyed the economies of most potential competitors [d] the unparalleled size of its workforce had given an impetus to its economy option a: american success is effortless, which is the opposite of painstaking; so it's not correct; option b: its domestic market was eight times larger than before changing the concept: the question is that the reason for america's success refers to its comparison with other civilizations, not its internal causes; option c: war destroys the development potential of potential competitors < the u.s. economy is the dream of european and asian peoples without directly mentioning "war destroys competitors"; option d: unparalleled modifies the scale of labor, whereas the original modifies the scale of the economy; so incorrect; step 4 : solving the problem question 2 question: 52. the loss of u.s. predominance in the world economy in the 1980 s is manifested in the fact that the american articles: it was inevitable that this primacy should have narrowed as other countries grew richer. just as inevitably, the retreat from predominance proved painful. analysis: as because the other countries grew richer followed is a sentence as indicates reason by the mid 1980s americans had found themselves at a loss over their fading industrial competitiveness. some huge american industries, such as consumer electronics, had shrunk or vanished in the face of foreign competition. key: had shrunk or vanished in the face of foreign competition american industry began to disappear when facing foreign competition; the following sentences start with examples; conclusion: 1. the content in parentheses must be read; 2. you cannot skip the content in the graduate entrance exam; step 5 : solve the problem question 3 title: what can be inferred from the passage？ [b] intense competition may contribute to economic progress. [d] a long history of success may pave the way for further development. content: all of this caused a crisis of confidence. americans stopped taking prosperity for granted. they began to believe that their way of doing business was failing, and that their incomes would therefore shortly begin to fall as well. the mid 1980 s brought one inquiry after another into the causes of america's industrial decline . their sometimes sensational findings were filled with warnings about the growing competition from overseas. analysis: all of this caused a crisis of confidence the crisis of americans loss of confidence; they began to believe that their way of doing business was failing the core of the sentence: failing indicates a negative meaning; core : this section centers on the that americans begin to deny their past; analysis: summary: translation requirements for the graduate entrance exam the general logic of the translated content is to be consistent with the article; step 6 : solving the problem question 4 analysis: keywords: while the main focus of the postgraduate entrance exam is " strong contrast relationship "; keywords: has been struggling intense struggle negative attitude; keywords: as followed by two noun concepts translated as "as" core sentences: self doubt has yielded to blind pride self doubt turns into blind confidence;

13.1.1 definition definition : discontinuity <font color=" ccc1d9" description:</font if $f(x)$ is defined in a punctured neighborhood of $x 0$ but is not continuous at $x 0$, then $x 0$ is a discontinuity of $f$. explanation 1. the function must be defined in some punctured neighborhood of $x 0$. 2. if it is not continuous at $x 0$, then $x 0$ is a discontinuity. classification of discontinuities 1. a discontinuity of the first kind: both one sided limits exist and are finite. removable discontinuity: the left and right hand limits are equal. jump discontinuity: the left and right hand limits are unequal. 2. a discontinuity of the second kind: at least one one sided limit does not exist as a finite number. infinite discontinuity: for example, $f(x)=1/x$ at $x=0$. oscillatory discontinuity: for example, $f(x)=\sin(1/x)$ at $x=0$. infinite and oscillatory discontinuities are common cases, but they are not the only possibilities. situations that commonly require one sided limits 1. boundary points of piecewise defined functions. 2. expressions involving $e^x$ as $x\to\pm\infty$. 3. expressions involving $\arctan x$ as $x\to\pm\infty$. 13.1.2 example problems example question : for $f(x)=\dfrac{\ln|x|}{|x 1|}\sin x$, find and classify its discontinuities. analysis the function is undefined at $x=0$ and $x=1$. at $x=0$, since $\sin x\sim x$ and $|x 1|\to1$, $$\lim {x\to0}\frac{\ln|x|}{|x 1|}\sin x =\lim {x\to0}x\ln|x|=0.$$ therefore, $x=0$ is a removable discontinuity. at $x=1$, since $\ln x\sim x 1$, $$\lim {x\to1^ }f(x)= \sin1,\qquad \lim {x\to1^+}f(x)=\sin1.$$ the one sided limits are finite but unequal, so $x=1$ is a jump discontinuity. question type: discontinuity

retained. mathematics graduate entrance examination mathematics advanced mathematics derivatives and differentials 1.1 definition of a differential 1.1.1 why differentials are useful core idea a differential is the linear part of a small change in a function. it approximates the actual increment when the independent variable increment is small. a derivative describes an instantaneous rate of change; a differential uses that rate to approximate an actual small change. example let $f(x)=x^2$. at $x 0$, $$\delta y=f(x 0+\delta x) f(x 0) =2x 0\delta x+(\delta x)^2.$$ as $\delta x\to0$, the term $(\delta x)^2$ is of higher order than $\delta x$, so $$\delta y\approx2x 0\delta x.$$ the linear term is the differential: $$dy=f'(x 0)\,dx=2x 0\delta x,\qquad dx=\delta x.$$ this approximation is useful in error estimation. pasted image 20231222204211 relationship between a derivative and a differential the derivative $f'(x 0)$ is the local rate of change. the actual increment is $\delta y=f(x 0+\delta x) f(x 0)$. the differential $dy=f'(x 0)\delta x$ is the linear principal part of $\delta y$. therefore, $$\frac{dy}{dx}=f'(x 0).$$ 1.1.2 formal definition definition : differential <font color=" ccc1d9" description:</font if $$f(x 0+\delta x) f(x 0)=a\delta x+o(\delta x)\qquad(\delta x\to0),$$ then $f$ is differentiable at $x 0$. its differential is $$dy=a\delta x.$$ explanation the term $a\delta x$ is the linear principal part of $\delta y$. the remainder $o(\delta x)$ is a higher order infinitesimal. hence $$\delta y=dy+o(\delta x),\qquad dy\approx\delta y.$$ geometric meaning for the curve $y=f(x)$, $dy=f'(x 0)dx$ is the vertical increment along the tangent line at $x 0$ corresponding to a horizontal increment $dx$. 1.1.3 differentiability and existence of the derivative theorem : differentiabilityandderivative <font color=" 8db3e2" <font color=" c6d9f0" description:</font </font for a single variable function, $f$ is differentiable at $x 0$ if and only if $f'(x 0)$ exists. in that case, $$dy=f'(x 0)\,dx.$$ 1.2 continuity, differentiability, and the derivative illustration pasted image 20240317192744 main relationships differentiability at $x 0$ implies continuity at $x 0$. continuity does not imply differentiability. for example, $f(x)=|x|$ is continuous at $0$, but its one sided derivatives are $ 1$ and $1$. existence of $f'(x 0)$ does not imply that $f'$ is continuous at $x 0$. existence of $f''(x 0)$ does not by itself imply that $\lim {x\to x 0}f''(x)$ exists. proof that differentiability implies continuity if $f'(x 0)$ exists, then $$\delta y=\frac{\delta y}{\delta x}\delta x.$$ as $\delta x\to0$, the difference quotient tends to the finite number $f'(x 0)$, while $\delta x\to0$. therefore $\delta y\to0$, which is continuity at $x 0$. pasted image 20240317190353 how to test differentiability if the function is discontinuous at the point, it is not differentiable there. if it is continuous, differentiability still must be checked: use the derivative definition; or verify that the left and right hand derivatives both exist and are equal. 1.2.2 repeated use of l'hôpital's rule 1. reapply the rule only while the expression remains of type $0/0$ or $\infty/\infty$ and all hypotheses of the rule continue to hold. 2. at every application, check that the derivative of the denominator is nonzero in a punctured neighborhood and that the new derivative ratio has a limit. 1.3 supplement: historical view of differentials 1.3.1 classical calculus characteristics pasted image 20240115172004 1. early calculus treated $dx$ and $dy$ as infinitesimal changes. 2. tangents were described using these infinitesimals. 3. the derivative was interpreted as the tangent slope $dy/dx$. pasted image 20240115171900 1.3.2 limit based definition limits provide a precise meaning for infinitesimals: a quantity is infinitesimal when its limit is zero. pasted image 20240115172055 modern interpretation in general, $dy$ is not identical to $\delta y$. instead, $$\delta y=dy+o(dx),\qquad dy\approx\delta y\quad(dx\to0).$$ thus the differential is the best linear approximation to the actual increment. pasted image 20240115172447

searchText: lecture 22: l’hôpital’s rule graduate entrance examination mathematics study notes: lecture 22: l’hôpital’s rule. original formulas, diagrams, and examples are retained. mathematics graduate entrance examination mathematics advanced mathematics mean value theorems and applications of derivatives 1.1 what is l'hôpital's rule? 1.1.1 basic concepts of l'hôpital's rule why l'hôpital's rule is needed using derivatives to calculate limits with indeterminate forms , mainly used for calculating indeterminate forms in fractional form; informally, l'hôpital's rule allows certain limits of the forms $0/0$ and $\infty/\infty$ to be evaluated through $\lim {x\to x 0}\frac{f(x)}{g(x)}=\lim {x\to x 0}\frac{f^{\prime}(x)}{g^{\prime}(x)}$, provided the rule's hypotheses are satisfied. its main advantage is that it can reduce certain quotient limits to simpler limits involving derivatives. more accessible explanation simply put, the essence of finding a limit is to compare the numerator and denominator with the order—to see who is faster. just like the numerator and denominator race toward zero or infinity on the track, we observers want to figure them out 1. who won? (is the limit greater than one or less than one?) ） 2. did they cross the finish line at the same time, or did the leader reach the finish line several lengths ahead? (same level or higher rank?) how much difference is there between crossing the line at the same time? (if they cross the line at the same level, what is the actual limit?) ） the problem is our visual judgment is limited: we know only how two quantities behave near a point. l'hôpital's rule says that, under specific hypotheses, comparing their derivatives can reveal the limiting ratio of the original quantities. each time you calculate the direction, the camera is half as slow; as it slows down, the process of crossing the finish line becomes increasingly clear; this slow motion analogy has limits: l'hôpital's rule cannot be used if the functions are not differentiable in the required punctured neighborhood, if the derivative ratio has no usable limit, or if the original expression is not of type $0/0$ or $\infty/\infty$. theorem : l'hôpital's rule <font color=" 8db3e2" <font color=" c6d9f0" description: </font </font if the following conditions are met: 1）$\lim {x\to x 0}f(x)=\lim {x\to x 0}g(x)=0;$ 2) $f(x)$ and $g(x)$ are differentiable within $\overset{\circ}{\operatorname {u}}(x 0, \delta)$, and $g^{\prime}(x)\neq0; $ 3) $\lim {x\to x 0}\frac{f^{\prime}(x)}{g^{\prime}(x)}$ exists (or $\infty)$ if the above conditions are met, then: $\lim {x\to x 0}\frac{f(x)}{g(x)}=\lim {x\to x 0}\frac{f^{\prime}(x)}{g^{\prime}(x)}$ explanation in short, it's the limit of the 0/0 type; proof : use cauchy's mean value theorem $\lim {x\to x {0}}\frac{f(x)}{f(x)}=\lim {x\to x {0}}\frac{f(x) f(x {0})}{g(x) g(x {0})}=\lim {x\to x {0}}\frac{f^{\prime}(\xi)}{g(\xi)}$ therefore, it equals $\lim {x\to x 0}\frac{f^{\prime}(x)}{g^{\prime}(x)}$ inference 1 : some secondary conclusions $x \sin x\sim\frac{1}{6}x^{3}$ ${\tan x\sim\frac13x^3}$ corollary 2 : when x approaches infinity, the growth rate is: $\log {a}x\ll x^{\alpha}\ll a^{\alpha}$ 1.1.2 example problems example question : $\text{ find the limit }\lim {x\to0}\frac{x^2+2\cos x 2}{\left(e^x 1\right)^2\ln(1+x^2)}$ analysis when the original expression is complex, the first consideration should be how to simplify it; analysis because $\begin{aligned}&\mathrm{e^x 1\sim x}\\&{\ln(1+x^2)\sim x^2}\end{aligned}$ so the original expression = $\lim {x\to x 0}\frac{x^{2}+2\cos x 2}{x^{4}}$ differentiate the numerator and denominator to obtain $\operatorname {lim} {x\rightarrow0}\frac{2x 2\sin x}{4x^{3}}=\frac{1}{2}\operatorname {lim} {x\rightarrow0}\frac{x \sin x}{x^{3}}$. at this point: you can use l'hôpital's rule. you can choose to substitute with equivalent value; use equivalent substitution at this point. the final result is 1/12; example : $\text{find }\lim {x\to+\infty}\frac{\log ax}{x^\alpha}\text{ and }\lim {x\to+\infty}\frac{x^\alpha}{a^x}.\ (a 1,\alpha 0)$ analysis both limits compare logarithmic, polynomial, and exponential growth rates. l'hôpital's rule can be applied. analysis 1. applying l'hôpital's rule once to the first limit gives $\lim {x\to\infty}\frac{\frac{1}{x\ln a}}{\alpha x^{\alpha 1}}=\lim {x\to\infty}\frac{1}{\alpha\ln a\,x^\alpha}=0$. 2. rewrite the second limit as $\lim {x\to+\infty}\frac{x^\alpha}{e^{x\ln a}}=0$. if using l'hôpital's rule, differentiate repeatedly until the power in the numerator is negative. conclusion as $x\to\infty$, the growth rates satisfy $\log {a}x\ll x^{\alpha}\ll a^{x}$. example : $\text{find }\lim {x\to0}\left[\frac1{\ln(1+x)} \frac1x\right].$ analysis this is an $\infty \infty$ indeterminate form. combining the terms produces a $\frac00$ form to which l'hôpital's rule applies. analysis $\lim {x\to0}\frac{x \ln(1+x)}{x\ln(1+x)}$ applying l'hôpital's rule twice gives $$\lim {x\to0}\frac{1 \frac1{1+x}}{\ln(1+x)+\frac{x}{1+x}} =\lim {x\to0}\frac{\frac1{(1+x)^2}}{\frac1{1+x}+\frac1{(1+x)^2}} =\frac12.$$ conclusion for infinity minus infinity problems, if there is a denominator, you can consider dividing by infinity by infinity type; example question : $\lim {x\to0^+}(x)^{\sin x}$ analysis analysis process: since the problem is zero to the power of zero , at this point transform into an exponential function with base e , then only count the exponent part and find the exponent's limit; analysis solution process: derived from the original expression = $\lim {x\to0^+}e^{\sin x\ln x}$ then find the exponent limit: $\lim {x\to0^+}\sin x\ln x$, then use equivalent substitution to change sinx x; $\lim {x\to0^{+}}x\ln x=\lim {x\to0^{+}}\frac{\log x}{\frac{1}{x}}=\lim {x\to0^{+}}\frac{\frac{1}{x}}{ \frac{1}{x^{2}}}=0$ conclusion 1. zero to the power of zero (including 1 to the power of infinite), convert it into exponential function with base e , find the limit of the exponent part; 2. 0 × infinity type, converts the 0 part into a denominator, then inverts it to become a denominator, making infinity a comparison to infinity; 1.2 situations where l'hôpital's rule is used 1.2.1 usage scenarios usage analysis : $\frac00;\quad\frac\infty\infty;\quad0\cdot\infty;\quad\infty \infty;\quad1^\infty;\quad\infty^0;\quad0^0$; the forms $\frac00$ and $\frac\infty\infty$ can be handled directly when the other hypotheses of l'hôpital's rule hold. the forms $0\cdot\infty$, $\infty \infty$, $1^\infty$, $\infty^0$, and $0^0$ must first be transformed into a quotient of type $\frac00$ or $\frac\infty\infty$. conversion rules : $\mathbf{0}\cdot\infty\quad\leftarrow\begin{cases}\mathbf{1}^{\infty}\\\infty^{0}\\\mathbf{0}^{0}&\end{cases}$ $\frac00,\frac\infty\infty\quad\leftarrow\begin{cases}0\cdot\infty&\leftarrow\begin{cases}1^\infty\\\infty^0\\0^0&\end{cases}&\end{cases}$ pasted image 20240111174212 1.2.2 notes 1. it needs to be simplified first by using equivalent substitution, it is replaced with a simpler form; 2. note condition 3 $\lim {x\to x 0}\frac{f^{\prime}(x)}{g^{\prime}(x)}$ exists (or $\infty)$ for example, $\lim {x\to+\infty}\frac{1 \cos x}{1+\cos x}$ does not exist because the expression oscillates and is unbounded near points where $1+\cos x=0$; l'hôpital's rule does not apply.

monotonicity 1.1.1 derivatives and monotonicity geometric illustration: relationship between the derivative and monotonicity theorem : derivatives and monotonicity let $f$ be continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable on $(a,b)$. 1. if $f'(x)\ge0$, then $f$ is nondecreasing on $[a,b]$. 2. if $f'(x)\le0$, then $f$ is nonincreasing on $[a,b]$. 3. if $f'(x) 0$, then $f$ is strictly increasing; if $f'(x)<0$, then $f$ is strictly decreasing. the condition $f'(x)\ge0$ together with only finitely many zeros of $f'$ is also sufficient for strict increase; the decreasing case is analogous. more generally, strict monotonicity follows if $f'$ is not identically zero on any subinterval. 1.1.2 examples example 1: determine the monotonic intervals of $f(x)=e^x x 1$ $$ f'(x)=e^x 1. $$ for $x<0$, $f'(x)<0$, so $f$ is strictly decreasing on $( \infty,0)$. for $x 0$, $f'(x) 0$, so $f$ is strictly increasing on $(0,+\infty)$. example 2: prove that $x \frac{x^3}{6}<\sin x<x$ for $x 0$ let $f(x)=x \sin x$. since $f(0)=0$ and $f'(x)=1 \cos x\ge0$, we have $f(x) 0$ for $x 0$, hence $\sin x<x$. let $g(x)=\sin x x+\frac{x^3}{6}$. then $g(0)=g'(0)=g''(0)=0$ and $$ g'''(x)=1 \cos x\ge0. $$ applying monotonicity successively gives $g''(x) 0$, $g'(x) 0$, and $g(x) 0$ for $x 0$. therefore $x \frac{x^3}{6}<\sin x$. 1.2 convexity and inflection points 1.2.1 definitions and the second derivative test definition : convexity let $f$ be continuous on an interval $i$. for any distinct $x 1,x 2\in i$: 1. if $$ f\left(\frac{x 1+x 2}{2}\right) < \frac{f(x 1)+f(x 2)}{2}, $$ then $f$ is strictly convex on $i$. 2. if the inequality is reversed, then $f$ is strictly concave on $i$. geometric meaning convex: each chord lies above the graph, and the slope increases. convex curve concave: each chord lies below the graph, and the slope decreases. concave curve theorem : second derivative test let $f$ be continuous on $[a,b]$ and twice differentiable on $(a,b)$. if $f''(x) 0$, then $f$ is convex on the interval. if $f''(x)<0$, then $f$ is concave on the interval. the sign of the first derivative determines monotonicity; the sign of the second derivative determines convexity or concavity. 1.2.2 inflection points definition : inflection point an inflection point is a point on a continuous curve where the curve changes from convex to concave or from concave to convex. candidate abscissas satisfy one of the following: 1. $f''(x 0)=0$; 2. $f''(x 0)$ does not exist, but $f$ is continuous at $x 0$. a candidate is not automatically an inflection point. the convexity must actually change across $x 0$. 1.2.3 examples example 1: determine the convexity of $y=x^3$ $$ y'=3x^2,\qquad y''=6x. $$ on $( \infty,0)$, $y''<0$, so the curve is concave. on $(0,+\infty)$, $y'' 0$, so the curve is convex. convexity changes across $x=0$, so $(0,0)$ is an inflection point. original illustration: inflection point of a cubic function example 2: find the convexity intervals and inflection point of $h(x)=\sqrt[3]{x}$ for $x\ne0$, $$ \begin{aligned} h'(x)&=\frac{1}{3}x^{ 2/3},\\ h''(x)&= \frac{2}{9}x^{ 5/3} = \frac{2}{9x^{5/3}}. \end{aligned} $$ for $x<0$, $h''(x) 0$, so the curve is convex. for $x 0$, $h''(x)<0$, so the curve is concave. although $h''(0)$ does not exist, $h$ is continuous at $0$ and the convexity changes there. thus $(0,0)$ is an inflection point. 1.3 common question types question type 1: convexity and inflection points 1. compute $f''(x)$. 2. find the points where $f''(x)=0$ or $f''(x)$ does not exist. 3. use these candidates to divide the domain and determine the sign of $f''$ on each interval. 4. a candidate is an inflection point only if the convexity changes across it. question type 2: number of roots existence: if $f$ is continuous on $[a,b]$ and $f(a)f(b)<0$, the intermediate value theorem guarantees at least one zero in $(a,b)$. uniqueness: if $f$ is strictly monotone on an interval, it has at most one zero there. rolle's theorem helps bound the number of roots: if $f$ has two distinct zeros, then $f'$ has at least one zero between them. question type 3: proving inequalities move all terms to one side, define an auxiliary function, and use its derivative to establish monotonicity. the lagrange mean value theorem is useful for differences of function values. for example, prove that for $x 0$, $$ \frac{x}{1+x}<\ln(1+x)<x. $$ let $f(x)=\ln(1+x) \frac{x}{1+x}$. then $$ f'(x)=\frac{x}{(1+x)^2} 0,\qquad f(0)=0, $$ so $f(x) 0$. next let $g(x)=x \ln(1+x)$. then $$ g'(x)=\frac{x}{1+x} 0,\qquad g(0)=0, $$ so $g(x) 0$. the desired inequality follows.

a differential equation is a mathematical equation used to describe the relationship between a function and its derivative . 1. its solution is not a number, but a function that fits the equations 2. the origin of differential equations dates back to the late 17th century, created to solve physical and astronomical problems encountered in the development of natural sciences; 3. a general equation representing the relationship between unknown functions, derivatives of unknown functions, and independent variables is called differential equations; 4. if the unknown function is a single variable function, it is called a ordinary differential equation ; if the unknown function is a multivariable function, it is called a partial differential equation ; 5. differential equations developed alongside calculus; 6. a differential equation contains equations of unknown functions and their derivatives; the highest order of the derivative of an unknown function is called the order of the differential equation; basic concepts differential equations: concept: equations containing unknown derivatives or differentials example: $y^{\prime}=y+x,y^{\prime\prime}+y^{3}=x,y^{\prime\prime}=e^{x}$ rank: concept: highest order containing the unknown function derivative ; example: when the differential equation is of order n: $f(x,y,y^{\prime},y^{(n)})=0$ solution: concept: if a function is substituted into a differential equation to make it an identity, then the function is called the solution to the differential equation. suppose: $y=y (x)$ is continuous on the interval i and has derivatives up to the $n$ order, so that $f[x, y (x), y^{\prime}(x), \cdotp\cdotp\cdotp, y^{(n)}(x)]\equiv 0, $ is called $y=y (x)$. the differential equation is in the interval a solution to $i.$ example: if the current differential equation is $y^{\prime\prime}=e^{x}$ then the solution to the current equation is: 1. this equation $y=e^{x}$ is the solution to the differential equation; 2. this equation $y=e^{x}+c {1}x+c {2}$ is also a solution to the differential equation; explanation: concept: if the solution to a differential equation contains any constant , and the number of independent (non combinable) constants equals the order of the differential equation, it is called a general solution to the equation; that is: the general solution represents the set of solutions, and the number of independent constants must equal the order of the differential equation; example: if there is a differential equation with a second order derivative $y^{\prime\prime}=3 ; y^{\prime}=3x+c {1}$ at this point, the function of y must have two constants: $y= rac{3}{2}x^{2}+c {1}x+c {2}$ particular solutions: concept: a solution containing no arbitrary constants is called a particular solution of the differential equation; supplement: assigning values to the arbitrary constants in the general solution produces a particular solution; to find the solution satisfying given initial conditions, first obtain the general solution and then determine its constants from those conditions; initial conditions: conditions used to determine a unique solution; integral curve: the graph of a solution is called an integral curve of the differential equation; the role of differential equations illustration: pasted image 20240422161204 definition : firstorderequation <font color=" ccc1d9" description: </font general form of first order equations: $y^\prime=f(x,y)$ definition : secondorderandhigherorderequations <font color=" ccc1d9" description: </font 1. second order differential equation: the highest derivative in an expression is the second order derivative; 2. higher order differential equations: equations containing third order derivatives, fourth order derivatives, or higher order derivatives; general form of a second order differential equation: $y^{\prime\prime}=f(x,y,y^{\prime})$ definition : ordinarydifferentialequations <font color=" ccc1d9" description: </font function has only one independent variable; explanation introduction: in physics: the most commonly used variable in ordinary differential modes is time; example: study the change in the position of a small ball after it is thrown upward; current differential equation: second order derivative gravitational acceleration of the ball $$\ddot{y}(t)= g$$ know first order derivatives : knowing that the downward component is gravitational acceleration $ g$, thus $\ddot{y}(t)= g$, its relationship with velocity can also be described: $ rac{d}{dt}( gt+v 0)= g$. acceleration alone does not determine the velocity; an initial condition is needed. add initial condition 1 : based on the speed of $v 0$, the downward g action is performed by $\dot{y}(t)= gt+v 0$ the position is still undetermined; at this stage we only know $ rac{d\,y(t)}{dt}= gt+v 0$. find an antiderivative : $ rac{d}{dt}\left(  rac{1}{2}gt^{2}+v {0}tight)= gt+v {0}$。 add initial condition 2 : when the initial position of an object is $y 0$ and its relationship is: $ rac{d}{dt}\left(  rac{1}{2}gt^{2}+v {0}t+y {0}ight)= gt+v {0}$. obtain the solution of the differential equation : $y(t)= (1/2)gt^2+v 0t+y 0$ definition : partialdifferentialequations <font color=" ccc1d9" description: </font function has multiple independent variables;
